description: Sunni caliphate ruling from Baghdad (750–1258) that displaced the Umayyads and presided over a golden age of Islamic learning, science, and administration; the House of Wisdom anchored a translation movement transmitting Greek philosophy to Europe, while Abbasid administrative models shaped successor states from Egypt to Central Asia.

temporal.notes: Ruled from Baghdad; ended with Mongol sack of Baghdad under Hulagu Khan

lifecycle_phases.description: Abbasids defeat Umayyads at Battle of the Zab; relocate capital to Baghdad (762); launch translation movement
Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun preside over the Islamic Golden Age; House of Wisdom founded; enormous territorial extent
Turkish military commanders gain real power; Buyid dynasty controls the caliph; peripheral regions break away
Caliphs retain religious prestige but no temporal power; Seljuks become de facto rulers; Baghdad sacked by Mongols 1258

rise_factors.description: Abbasids claimed descent from the Prophet's uncle Abbas, lending sacred legitimacy to their rule over all Muslims
Created a sophisticated bureaucracy incorporating Persian administrative traditions; established a professional standing army
Baghdad at the hub of Silk Road trade; controlled maritime routes from Persian Gulf to Indian Ocean

The Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad became the world's premier intellectual institution, translating Greek philosophical and scientific texts into Arabic and producing original scholarship in mathematics (al-Khwarizmi's algebra), astronomy, and medicine.

At its height (9th century), Baghdad was the world's largest city with over 1 million inhabitants. Its position at the junction of Tigris/Euphrates trade routes made it the clearinghouse for commerce between the Mediterranean, Central Asia, and the Indian Ocean.

The Abbasids adopted Sassanid Persian administrative models: wazirs (viziers), diwan (state bureaus), and complex bureaucratic traditions. This institutional transplant gave Islamic governance a capacity for large-scale administration absent in earlier Arab tribal structures.

decline_factors.description: Repeated succession crises and civil wars between caliphal factions weakened central authority
Buyid, Fatimid, Seljuk, and numerous other dynasties carved out autonomous or independent rule from Abbasid territory
Mongol military machine under Hulagu Khan overwhelmed Abbasid defenses; Baghdad sacked 1258, ending the caliphate

Caliph al-Mutasim's recruitment of Turkish ghulam soldiers (833) proved fatal: by 861 Turkish commanders were murdering caliphs at will. The Abbasid caliphs became figureheads while successive Turkish dynasties (Buyid, Seljuk) held actual power.

Hulagu Khan's sack of Baghdad (1258) killed Caliph al-Musta'sim and an estimated 200,000–800,000 inhabitants. The destruction of the irrigation system depopulated formerly agricultural Mesopotamia for centuries, ending the Abbasid caliphate as a territorial power.

description: Indigenous people of northern Japan, Sakhalin, and the Kuril Islands whose Ainu language, bear ceremonialism, and salmon-fishing culture were distinct from mainland Japanese civilisation; the Ainu inhabited Hokkaido and adjacent islands as hunter-gatherers and traders of furs and seafood integrated into Japanese, Chinese, and later Russian commercial networks before Meiji-era colonisation suppressed their cultural autonomy.

geographic.no_central_capital_reason: Decentralised hunter-gatherer society; no fixed capital.

lifecycle_phases.description: Ainu ancestors inhabited Hokkaido and parts of Honshu; semi-nomadic hunter-gatherer economy based on salmon, deer, and bear.
Distinctive Ainu culture crystallised with elaborate bear ceremonies, oral tradition (yukar epics), and extensive trade with mainland Japan and the continent.
Japanese expansion northward from Honshu compressed Ainu territory; conflict with Wajin settlers increased and trading relationships became more asymmetric.

rise_factors.description: Dense forests and island geography of Hokkaido shielded Ainu communities from full conquest.
Rich salmon runs and marine resources supported dense populations relative to climate.
Shared animist cosmology and bear-ceremony ritual cycle bound dispersed communities.

decline_factors.description: Sustained Wajin colonisation from southern Honshu progressively displaced Ainu from productive coastal lowlands.
Incorporation into Japanese trade networks eroded Ainu economic autonomy.
Epidemic disease introduced via expanding contact with Japanese merchants reduced population.

religion: Christianity (Ethiopian Orthodox tradition from c.330 CE)

population_estimates.note: Highland and coastal combined; speculative.
Post-Arab-conquest contraction.

description: The Aksumite Empire (c.100–940 CE) was a major trading power on the horn of Africa, controlling the Red Sea coast and projecting influence into Yemen during the 6th century. Aksum was one of the first states to adopt Christianity (under King Ezana, c.330 CE), later than Armenia but earlier than the Roman Empire's general conversion. The kingdom minted its own gold, silver, and bronze coinage, extremely rare for sub-Saharan Africa, and Aksumite stelae remain among the largest single-stone monuments ever erected. Trade flowed through the port of Adulis, linking the Indian Ocean spice trade to Mediterranean buyers. The empire's decline coincided with the rise of Arab/Umayyad maritime dominance after the 7th century, which choked Adulis. Successor Christian kingdoms (Zagwe, later the Solomonic dynasty) inherited the Ge'ez language and the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition Aksum had founded.

internal_structure.legitimacy_basis: divine kingship; after 330 CE Christian anointment
internal_structure.administrative_system: subordinate sub-kings (nagasi) under a single negus negast (king of kings)

lifecycle_phases.description: Unification of pre-Aksumite chiefdoms under one royal line.
Christianization under Ezana, gold coinage, Yemen invasion under Kaleb.
Loss of Yemeni territory; Red Sea trade choked by Arab fleets.
Capital shifts inland; political authority dissolves into Zagwe successor.

rise_factors.description: Port of Adulis dominated Red Sea trade between Roman/Byzantine buyers and Indian Ocean producers.
Ezana's conversion c.330 CE allied Aksum diplomatically with Byzantine Constantinople.
Kaleb's 525 CE invasion of Himyarite Yemen demonstrated cross-Red-Sea power projection.

decline_factors.description: Umayyad/Arab maritime dominance after 640s diverted Indian Ocean trade away from Adulis.
Centuries of plough agriculture on Tigrayan highlands eroded soils, reducing surplus.
Beja and Agaw raids on the northern frontier strained the late-period army.

key_figures.name: Ezana
key_figures.notes: First Christian Aksumite monarch.

key_figures.name: Kaleb
key_figures.notes: Invaded Yemen to protect Christian Himyarites.

key_figures.name: Gersem
key_figures.notes: Last attested coinage-issuing Aksumite monarch.

description: Iranian nomadic confederation (c. 1st–15th c.) originating in the steppe north of the Caucasus; Hunnic pressure drove Alan groups westward into Europe during the Migration Period, some reaching Iberia and North Africa, while eastern Alans in the Caucasus established the Alania kingdom that adopted Orthodox Christianity; the Alans' descendants are the modern Ossetians of the central Caucasus.

temporal.notes: Stub: dates from GeoJSON basemap years 700–1100

lifecycle_phases.description: Iranian-speaking Alans dominated the steppes north of the Caucasus and Caspian, raiding into Persia and the Roman East.
Hunnic invasion shattered Alan unity; remnant groups migrated westward with Gothic federations into Gaul and Spain.
Alan fragments established short-lived settlements in Gaul and north Africa before being absorbed by Visigoths and Vandals.
Alans in the Caucasus (ancestors of modern Ossetians) maintained independence under Khazar and later Byzantine overlordship.

rise_factors.description: Alan heavy cavalry tactics made them feared mercenaries and raiders across late antiquity.
Command of the Pontic steppe gave access to vast pastures and rapid strategic mobility.

decline_factors.description: Mongol invasions of 1222-1239 devastated the Caucasian Alans and ended their political independence.
Diaspora groups in western Europe were rapidly assimilated into dominant host cultures.

description: Berber reform movement that crossed from North Africa (1147) to reunify Muslim Iberia under strict Maliki doctrine; at its peak ruled all of al-Andalus and the Maghreb, but defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) irreversibly broke Almohad power and opened Andalusia to Castilian reconquest.

temporal.notes: Defeated at Las Navas de Tolosa 1212; collapse follows

lifecycle_phases.description: Almohad forces from Morocco cross into Iberia, eliminate the taifa kingdoms and Almoravid remnants, and unify Muslim Iberia under a single puritanical Berber caliphate. Córdoba, Seville, and Granada fall to Almohad control.

Caliph Yaqub al-Mansur defeats Alfonso VIII at Alarcos (1195), inflicting the worst Christian defeat in the Reconquista. The defeat temporarily checks Christian expansion and forces the Christian kingdoms to form a coalition.

Coalition of Castile, Aragon, Navarre, and Portugal crushes Almohad forces at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), a decisive turning point in the Reconquista. Internal Almohad succession crises and Berber tribal revolts shatter unity. Seville (1248) and other cities fall to Castile.

rise_factors.description: Almohad ('those who affirm divine unity') ideology offered a reformist Islamic challenge to both Almoravid perceived laxity and Christian expansion; puritanical religious zeal motivated military jihad and political consolidation

Almohad armies combined Berber tribal cavalry from Morocco with Iberian Muslim infantry; their unified command under the caliph solved the coordination problems that had doomed the fragmented taifa states

The Almohads (al-Muwahhidun = "those who affirm divine unity") launched a strict Maliki reform movement against Berber popular religion and Iberian Muslim laxity, mobilizing religious enthusiasm that sustained rapid conquest.

The Battle of Alarcos (1195) destroyed a Castilian army and forced Alfonso VIII to surrender dozens of fortresses. This victory demonstrated Almohad peak military power and temporarily halted the Reconquista.

Despite its religious intolerance, the Almohad period paradoxically stimulated philosophical and medical scholarship: Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Maimonides (both born in Córdoba) pursued their work partly in response to Almohad intellectual challenges.

The Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur's crushing victory at Alarcos (1195) over Alfonso VIII of Castile temporarily reversed Reconquista momentum and demonstrated the revitalized Islamic military capacity under Almohad discipline.

decline_factors.description: Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) broke Almohad military supremacy; the Christian coalition showed that Iberian kingdoms could coordinate effectively. Ferdinand III of Castile then conquered Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248) in rapid succession.
Almohad succession was disputed between family branches; the empire's North African base fragmented under Hafsid, Marinid, and Zayyanid challengers, removing support for the Iberian caliphate

The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), a combined Christian crusade force, shattered the Almohad army and opened Andalucia to rapid Christian conquest. Within 40 years, only Granada remained under Muslim rule.

Almohad authority rested on a Berber tribal confederation that proved fragile under military stress. Defeats triggered tribal secession; the Hafsids, Zayyanids, and Marinids all broke away as regional powers in the 1230s.

sources.title: Kingdoms of Faith: A New History of Islamic Spain

description: Sanhaja Berber confederation from the western Sahara that intervened in Iberia (1086) at the invitation of taifa kings threatened by Alfonso VI of Castile; reunited fragmented taifas under austere Maliki rule and checked Christian expansion for half a century before internal decay and Almohad succession.

temporal.notes: Berber dynasty extending from Maghreb

lifecycle_phases.description: Taifa kings invite Almoravids from Morocco after Alfonso VI captures Toledo (1085). Yusuf ibn Tashfin defeats Alfonso VI at Sagrajas (1086), halting Christian expansion. Almoravids then conquer the taifa kingdoms themselves, replacing fragmented rule with unified Berber government.

Almoravid empire spans Morocco to Iberia to West African gold fields but cannot hold all fronts simultaneously. Christian reconquest resumes under Alfonso I of Aragon; Lisbon raided. Internal religious reformers (future Almohads) challenge Almoravid legitimacy in Morocco.

rise_factors.description: Almoravid camel-mounted and shock infantry tactics, combined with North African reinforcements, reversed the Christian military advantage; Sagrajas (1086) proved Berber armies superior to Iberian Christian cavalry in pitched battle

Almoravids offered religious orthodoxy (Maliki jurisprudence) and jihad against Christian expansion, giving fragmented taifa Muslims a unifying Islamic identity they had lost under competing petty kings

The Almoravid movement began as a Maliki Islamic reform among Sanhaja Berbers of the Sahara. Rigid adherence to orthodox Sunni practice gave the movement a disciplined, motivated core that regular Iberian Muslim armies lacked.

The Battle of Sagrajas (1086) routed Alfonso VI's Castilian army, rescuing Iberian Muslim taifa kingdoms from imminent collapse and demonstrating that organized Berber infantry could defeat Iberian heavy cavalry.

Almoravid heartlands in the western Sahara controlled trans-Saharan gold trade routes. Gold from Mali/Ghana reached Iberia and Europe via Almoravid merchants, funding military expansion and urban development.

decline_factors.description: Maintaining simultaneous campaigns in Iberia, Morocco, and the Saharan trade routes overstretched Almoravid military and administrative resources; the Strait of Gibraltar crossing created perpetual logistical vulnerability

Almohad religious reform movement arose in Morocco (1120s) and challenged Almoravid legitimacy; by 1147 the Almohads had conquered all of Morocco, leaving the Iberian Almoravids isolated from their base

Iberian Muslims resented Almoravid severity: banning music, burning philosophic texts, and imposing Saharan practices. Urban Al-Andalus educated classes actively collaborated with the Almohad replacement.

The Almohad movement defeated the Almoravids first in Morocco (1147), cutting their supply lines, before completing the conquest of Iberia. The Almoravids faced a two-front war against both Christians and Almohad Berbers.

The Almohad reformers condemned the Almoravids as theologically insufficiently rigorous; their military campaigns from North Africa swept the Almoravid emirs out of Iberia between 1147 and 1172 with the support of Andalusi religious scholars.

description: Nubian Christian kingdom (c. 5th–16th c.) south of Makuria centred on Soba on the Blue Nile; the southernmost of the Nubian Christian kingdoms, Alwa maintained diplomatic relations with Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa while preserving Meroitic cultural elements; its later conversion to Islam and eventual absorption into the Funj Sultanate (c. 1504) ended sub-Saharan Christian Nubian political identity.

geographic.no_central_capital_reason: Capital location uncertain; possibly Soba but no centralised polity.

lifecycle_phases.description: Alodia/Alwa emerged as a Nubian Christian kingdom along the Blue Nile confluence; received Coptic Christianity via Axum and Egypt.
Peak period of church construction and trans-Saharan trade; capital Soba was a major city with large stone churches.
Arab migration into Nubia increased pressure; Islamisation of trade networks marginalised the Christian kingdom.
Final collapse under pressure from Funj Sultanate and Arab nomadic incursions; Soba was destroyed c. 1504.

rise_factors.description: Coptic Christianity provided administrative cohesion and literary culture connecting Alwa to Byzantium and Axum.
Position at Blue Nile confluence enabled taxation of trade between sub-Saharan Africa and Egypt.

decline_factors.description: Shift of trans-Saharan commerce toward Muslim-dominated networks excluded Christian Nubia.
Arab nomadic incursions eroded agricultural base and border security.
Succession crises weakened central authority in the final century.

description: Collective term for the competing kingdoms, Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, Wessex, that dominated post-Roman Britain (c. 600–850); their dynastic rivalries, shifting overlordships, and ecclesiastical networks formed the political substrate from which the unified English monarchy eventually emerged.

temporal.notes: Collective term for the early Anglo-Saxon kingdoms; flagged for review

geographic.no_central_capital_reason: Umbrella term for seven distinct kingdoms, each with its own seat.

lifecycle_phases.description: Germanic peoples, Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, migrate to Roman Britain after the Roman withdrawal (410), gradually pushing the Britons westward into Wales and Cornwall. Seven major kingdoms emerge (the 'Heptarchy'): Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex. Christianity returns to England through Augustine of Canterbury's mission (597), sent by Pope Gregory the Great.

Overlordship (bretwaldaship) rotates among the dominant kingdoms: Northumbria's Æthelfrith and Edwin, then Mercia's Penda and Offa. King Offa of Mercia (757–796) is the most powerful Anglo-Saxon king before Alfred; he corresponds with Charlemagne as an equal and builds Offa's Dyke, the greatest Anglo-Saxon construction project, to mark the Welsh-English border. Northumbrian monasteries (Lindisfarne, Jarrow) produce the Lindisfarne Gospels and Bede's Ecclesiastical History.

The Great Heathen Army (865) systematically destroys the Heptarchy: Northumbria falls (866), East Anglia (869, King Edmund martyred), and Mercia is occupied (877). Only Wessex under Alfred the Great survives. The Treaty of Wedmore (878) creates the Danelaw in the north and east of England. The Heptarchy as a political system ends; England is now divided between Viking Danelaw and West Saxon Christian England.

rise_factors.description: The conversion of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms to Christianity (597–650s) brought them into the European political order and provided administrative literacy through the Church; Northumbrian monasticism produced the most sophisticated scholarly culture in 7th-8th century Europe

England's island geography provided protection from Frankish and Carolingian expansion; while the Anglo-Saxons suffered Viking raids, the island setting prevented the kind of total conquest that eliminated Continental Germanic kingdoms

The concept of Bretwalda (over-king) created a mechanism for aspiring rulers to claim authority over multiple kingdoms, driving cycles of political centralization as dominant kingdoms absorbed weaker neighbors.

The conversion of Anglo-Saxon kingdoms to Christianity (597–686) introduced literate clergy who wrote charters, administered estates, and preserved laws, dramatically increasing state capacity across all the kingdoms.

Anglo-Saxon kingdoms developed silver sceat coinage independently (c.680–750), facilitating market exchange across the Heptarchy and enabling tax collection in coin rather than kind, a major administrative advance.

The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms produced some of early medieval Europe's most advanced scholars, Bede's Ecclesiastical History (731) established a model of historical writing that influenced all subsequent medieval historiography.

decline_factors.description: The Great Heathen Army's strategy was systematically different from earlier Viking raids: instead of raiding and leaving, the army wintered in England and conquered territory; the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms lacked the fortified infrastructure and mobile reserves to respond effectively
The Heptarchy's seven competing kingdoms could not sustain unified resistance; each kingdom fell to the Danes in sequence while potential allies watched or were themselves threatened

The Great Heathen Army (865–878) systematically conquered Northumbria (866), East Anglia (869), and Mercia (874), destroying three of the seven heptarchic kingdoms within a decade and leaving only Wessex intact.

Alfred the Great and his successors used the Danish wars as justification for absorbing remaining kingdoms: Mercia came under Æthelflæd, East Anglia and Northumbria were reconquered, ending the multi-kingdom Heptarchy model.

sources.author: Reuter, Timothy (ed.)
sources.title: The New Cambridge Medieval History, Vol. III: c. 900 – c. 1024

description: Vietnamese kingdom in the Red River delta (968–1407, 1427–1804) that maintained independence from Chinese absorption through military resistance and cultural adaptation of Chinese administrative forms; the Lý and Trần dynasties sponsored Buddhist monuments and developed a distinctive Sino-Vietnamese literary culture while repelling three Mongol invasions (1258, 1285, 1288); the Later Lê dynasty's victory over Ming occupation (1427) reasserted Vietnamese sovereignty.

temporal.notes: Span covers Ngô-Đinh-Lê-Lý-Trần-Hồ era from Bạch Đằng victory (939, end of Chinese rule) to Ming conquest of Đại Ngu (1407). Original stub was 1000–1000 from GeoJSON basemap snapshot.

lifecycle_phases.description: Đinh Bộ Lĩnh defeats local warlords; Lý dynasty established (1009) at Thăng Long (Hanoi); independence from Tang Chinese culture asserted
Lý dynasty's Buddhist temple building; defeat of Song Chinese invasion (1077); advance into Champa territory southward
Trần dynasty; three Mongol invasions repelled (1258, 1285, 1288) by guerrilla tactics; Ming Chinese occupation (1407–1427)
Lê Lợi expels Ming forces; Later Lê dynasty codifies Hong Duc legal code; Vietnamese literary culture expands

rise_factors.description: Vietnamese guerrilla tactics, using river valleys, monsoon flooding, and scorched-earth retreat, defeated three Mongol invasions that overwhelmed all other Asian opponents
Red River delta's terrain and Vietnam's elongated coastal geography provided strategic depth against Chinese northern invasion pressure

decline_factors.description: Ming Chinese military technology and administrative capacity proved capable of overwhelming Vietnamese resistance during the 1407–1427 occupation period

description: Armenian kingdom (ancient – medieval) in the South Caucasus whose conversion to Christianity (301 CE) made it the first Christian state in the world; Armenian political history alternated between Persian, Byzantine, Arab, Mongol, and Turkish overlordship while Armenian cultural identity was preserved through the unique Armenian alphabet (created 405 CE), the Apostolic Church, and a literate merchant diaspora that spread from the Mediterranean to India.

temporal.notes: Stub: dates from GeoJSON basemap years 700–1200

lifecycle_phases.description: Armenian nobility (nakharars) maintained semi-independence under alternating Byzantine and Sasanian suzerainty.
Arab conquest ended Arsacid rule; Armenians endured as subordinate marzpanate while preserving church and alphabet.
Bagratid dynasty unified Armenian principalities and established a cultural renaissance centred on Ani.
Seljuk conquest of Ani (1064) dispersed Armenians; diaspora communities formed the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia in the south.
Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia flourished as a Crusader-era maritime state until Mamluk conquest in 1375.

rise_factors.description: Armenian Apostolic Church and unique alphabet created cultural identity resistant to conquest.
Mountain terrain of the Armenian Plateau impeded full conquest by any single power.
Bagratid dynasty effectively united nakharar nobility under a single crown.

decline_factors.description: Permanent location between Byzantine, Sasanian, Arab, and Seljuk powers meant constant military pressure.
Fall of Ani in 1064 ended Armenian statehood in the homeland for centuries.
Cilician Armenia's survival depended on Crusader support that evaporated after Acre fell (1291).

description: Armenian polity established in mountainous Cilicia by refugees from Seljuk-conquered Greater Armenia (1080–1375); a crucial Crusader ally supplying intelligence, provisioning, and dynastic ties, it maintained Christian sovereignty between the Latin states and Byzantium until extinguished by Mamluk conquest.

temporal.notes: Crusader-era Armenian polity in Cilicia; falls to Mamluks 1375.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Ruben I establishes Armenian principality in the Taurus as Byzantine power fragments.
Territorial growth and Crusader alliance during the First and Second Crusades.
Leo I crowned king 1198; kingdom at maximum extent and international recognition.
Mamluk raids destroy lowland revenues; kingdom retreats to highland core.
Final Mamluk conquest; Leon V dies in exile 1393.

rise_factors.description: Taurus Mountains protected the kingdom against Byzantine, Seljuk, and later Crusader pressures, making the highland core nearly impregnable.
Alliance with the Crusader states provided military cooperation and commercial partners in the eastern Mediterranean.
Rubenid then Hethumid dynasties consolidated Armenian noble families, creating durable governing coalitions.

Armenian Cilicia served as the primary provisioning base for the Crusader states: Antioch, Tripoli, and Edessa all depended on Armenian food exports and military cooperation. This strategic value generated both revenue and political protection from Crusader military power.

Armenian rulers of Cilicia cultivated close ties with western European powers, through marriage, crusade cooperation, and political alliance, as a counterweight to Turkish and Egyptian pressure. This alignment provided intermittent diplomatic support from the papacy and France.

Cilicia became the center of Armenian ecclesiastical life after the collapse of Bagratid Armenia. The Catholicos (head of the Armenian Apostolic Church) relocated to Sis, making Cilicia both the political and spiritual center of Armenian civilization in exile.

decline_factors.description: Mamluk invasions repeatedly devastated lowland territories from 1266 onward, progressively stripping the kingdom of its economic base.
Western crusading support collapsed after the fall of Acre 1291, leaving Cilicia isolated against Mamluk pressure.
Mamluk conquest 1375 ended independent Armenian rule.

Mamluk campaigns progressively stripped Cilicia of territory from the 1260s onward. Each successive Mamluk sultan took more Armenian fortresses; the fall of Sis (1375) to Barquq ended Armenian statehood, and the royal family fled west as refugees.

Cilicia' Mongol alliance (1247) provided temporary protection but also made it an Ilkhanate tributary. When the Ilkhanate fragmented (1335), Cilicia lost its great-power protector and faced Mamluk expansion without military support.

description: Small island kingdom in the Firth of Clyde historically contested between the Kingdom of the Isles and the Scottish crown; its strategic position at the mouth of the Clyde made it important for western Scottish naval operations, and the island passed to Scotland through the Treaty of Perth (1266) that transferred the Hebrides from Norwegian to Scottish sovereignty.

temporal.notes: Stub: dates from GeoJSON basemap years 1000–1100

lifecycle_phases.description: Isle of Arran formed part of the Dál Riata kingdom and later early Scottish realm.
Viking raids and settlement brought Norse culture and place names; Arran passed between Norse and Scottish overlordship.
Gradually incorporated into the Scottish kingdom following the 1263 Treaty of Perth which ceded the Western Isles.

rise_factors.description: Strategic position in the Firth of Clyde made Arran important for control of western sea lanes.

decline_factors.description: Small size and island geography kept Arran permanently subordinate to larger mainland powers.

description: Steppe empire that dominated the middle Danube basin (c. 567–803) after driving out the Lombards and Gepids; conducted devastating joint raids with Slavs deep into Frankish and Byzantine territory and besieged Constantinople (626) before fragmentation by Charlemagne's campaigns destroyed the khaganate and opened the Carpathian basin to Slavic settlement.

temporal.notes: Pannonian steppe empire; destroyed by Carolingian campaigns.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Bayan I leads Avars into Pannonia, displacing Gepids and establishing the khaganate.
Siege of Constantinople 626; peak Avar military reach into Italy and Byzantine Balkans.
Control of Pannonia and Dacia; Slavic peoples incorporated as subordinate federates.
Avar power wanes; Byzantine subsidies reduced; Slavic federates grow more autonomous.
Charlemagne's campaigns destroy the ring-forts; remaining Avars assimilated or scattered.

rise_factors.description: Avar heavy cavalry dominated the open Pannonian plain; strategic depth allowed rapid concentration against any threat.
Byzantine Empire paid large annual gold subsidies to Avars through the 7th century, financing the khaganate.
Avars spread stirrup technology westward, giving their cavalry a decisive positional advantage over opponents.

The Avars introduced the iron stirrup to Europe, enabling fully armored cavalry warfare. Stirruped cavalry could deliver lance charges with full body weight, a military technology that transformed European warfare for centuries and gave Avar armies decisive tactical superiority.

At its height, the Avar Khaganate extracted annual tribute payments from Byzantium (typically gold solidi), Frankish kingdoms, and subject Slavic peoples. This tributary system generated wealth from military threats rather than requiring productive agricultural management.

decline_factors.description: Charlemagne launched systematic campaigns 791–804, destroying the ring-forts and capturing the treasure hoard.
Kaghan succession disputes weakened central authority before the Frankish campaigns began.
Frankish settlement of Pannonia and Slavic expansion erased the Avar political and demographic presence.

Charlemagne's systematic campaigns against the Avars (791–803) captured the Ring (hring), the fortified treasury storing generations of tribute, and distributed enormous wealth to Frankish nobles. The military destruction was so complete that the Avar name disappeared from Pannonia within decades.

The Avars' Slavic subject population outnumbered them throughout the khaganate. After the Frankish military defeats, Slavic peoples absorbed the surviving Avar population rather than vice versa, leaving no detectable Avar cultural legacy.

sources.author: Morgan, David
sources.title: The Mongols

description: Sunni Kurdish dynasty founded by Saladin (1171) that reunified Egypt, Syria, and the Jazira under a single strategic command; its conquest of Jerusalem (1187) remade the Crusader states' political geography and its sophisticated administrative devolution into appanages for family princes created the fragmentation later exploited by the Mongols and Mamluks.

temporal.notes: Founded by Saladin; unites Egypt and Syria; Saladin retakes Jerusalem 1187; dynasty fragments after Saladin's death; last Ayyubid rulers ousted by Mamluks in Egypt (1250) and in Syria (1260)

lifecycle_phases.description: Saladin abolishes the Fatimid Caliphate (1171), reuniting Egypt with Sunni orthodoxy; defeats Crusaders at Hattin (1187) and retakes Jerusalem; repels Third Crusade at Acre; dies 1193 having reunited the Islamic Near East

Saladin's empire divided among his brothers and sons; multiple Ayyubid sultans in Egypt, Damascus, Aleppo, and Yemen pursue independent policies; Fifth and Sixth Crusades negotiated away; al-Kamil cedes Jerusalem to Frederick II (1229)

Egyptian Ayyubids overthrown by their own Mamluk slave-soldiers (1250); Ayyubid princes survive in Hama and other Syrian cities until Mongol invasions and Mamluk consolidation eliminate remaining branches by 1341

rise_factors.description: Saladin combined Kurdish tribal forces with professional Syrian and Egyptian armies into a coherent command structure; his siege warfare ended Crusader castle dominance at key fortresses

Saladin cultivated the image of the ideal Sunni ruler defending Islam against Crusaders and the heretical Fatimids; retaking Jerusalem in 1187 gave enormous religious prestige throughout the Islamic world
Exploited the Crusader states' internal succession crises (Baldwin IV's leprosy, disputed regencies) and the Fatimid caliphate's weakness to build a unified Egyptian-Syrian power base

Saladin eliminated Fatimid Shiism from Egypt (1171) and reunited Egypt, Syria, and Mesopotamia under Sunni rule for the first time since the 10th century. This reunification concentrated resources that had been divided between rival caliphates.

The Battle of Hattin (1187) annihilated the Kingdom of Jerusalem's field army and captured its True Cross relic. The subsequent capture of Jerusalem triggered the Third Crusade but demonstrated that sustained Muslim military mobilization could reverse Crusader territorial gains.

The Treaty of Jaffa (1229), Al-Kamil's negotiation with Frederick II, returned Jerusalem without military loss. This diplomatic flexibility, sacrificing territory for peace to address internal threats, demonstrated sophisticated foreign policy realism.

decline_factors.description: Saladin's practice of dividing territories among relatives created endemic fragmentation; Ayyubid princes frequently allied with Crusaders against each other, destroying the dynasty's anti-Crusader unity

The Mamluks (slave-soldier elite created by the Ayyubids themselves) developed superior military cohesion; Egyptian Mamluks overthrew Sultan Turanshah immediately after defeating the Seventh Crusade at Mansura

Saladin's practice of distributing provinces to family members created permanent Ayyubid sub-dynasties in Damascus, Aleppo, Homs, Hamah, and Yemen. These relatives cooperated occasionally but competed chronically, preventing unified military response to both Crusaders and Mongols.

The Mamluk slave-soldiers, brought in for military strength, overthrew Sultan Turanshah (1250) just after defeating the Seventh Crusade. This military coup ended Ayyubid rule in Egypt and inaugurated the Mamluk sultanate, which rapidly absorbed remaining Ayyubid territories.

population_estimates.note: Deccan plateau under Bahmani administration; estimates from Habib and Raychaudhuri.

description: Muslim Deccan sultanate (1347–1527) founded by Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah, an officer of the Tughluq Sultanate who revolted at Daulatabad after the Delhi Sultanate's expansion into the south had overextended its administration; the Bahmanis ruled the Deccan plateau north of the Tungabhadra from Gulbarga and later Bidar, fought protracted wars with the Vijayanagara Empire over the Raichur Doab, became the principal Persianate Islamic state of the Indian subcontinent through patronage of architecture, calligraphy, and Persian court culture, and built the Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan (1472); from the late 15th century the sultanate fragmented into the five Deccan successor states (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar) that would later combine to defeat Vijayanagara at Talikota (1565).

temporal.notes: Founded by Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah after the Daulatabad rebellion against the Tughluq Sultanate; fragmented into the five Deccan sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar) from c. 1490; finally extinguished 1527.

lifecycle_phases.description: Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah declares independence from the Tughluq Sultanate at Daulatabad; capital established at Gulbarga; first wars with Vijayanagara.
Vizier Mahmud Gawan reforms the army, divides the empire into administrative tarafs, and conducts the Konkan campaigns that bring the Bahmani sultanate to its maximum extent.

Execution of Mahmud Gawan (1481) triggers factionalism; provincial governors progressively assert autonomy as the five Deccan sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar) emerge from the Bahmani frame.

description: Baltic-speaking peoples of the eastern Baltic (Prussians, Latvians, Lithuanians, Latvians, Semigallians) whose late Christianisation, Lithuania's paganism lasted until 1387, made the eastern Baltic the last frontier of medieval Crusading; Baltic cultures maintained distinctive polytheistic religions, amber trade networks, and agricultural societies that resisted both German Teutonic Order conquest and Christian assimilation.

temporal.notes: Pre-state Baltic-speaking peoples (Prussians, Lithuanians, Latvians, Semigallians) before consolidation into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and absorption by the Teutonic Order; later dates handled by teutonic_order_state and grand_duchy_of_lithuania.

lifecycle_phases.description: Baltic peoples (Latvians, Lithuanians, Prussians, Curonians) occupied the eastern Baltic littoral as independent tribal confederations.
Increasing pressure from Viking raids, early Russian principalities, and Polish expansion threatened tribal independence.
Northern Crusades led by Teutonic Knights and Livonian Order subjugated most Baltic tribes; Lithuanians alone formed a lasting kingdom.

rise_factors.description: Dense forests and marshes of the Baltic littoral made conquest logistically difficult.
Control of Baltic amber trade provided economic resources for weapons and alliance-building.

decline_factors.description: German and Danish crusaders with castles and professional knights overwhelmed tribal war bands.
Lack of unified political structure made coordinated resistance impossible.

description: First Bulgarian Empire (681–1018) founded when Asparuh's Bulgars crossed the Danube and established a state mixing Bulgar nomadic aristocracy with Slavic peasant population; Boris I's conversion to Christianity (864) established Bulgaria in the Byzantine cultural orbit while Simeon I's military campaigns made Bulgaria the dominant Balkan power and his Preslav court pioneered Slavonic literary culture in Cyrillic script.

temporal.notes: Stub: dates from GeoJSON basemap years 1000–1400

lifecycle_phases.description: Asparuh's Bulgars cross Danube and defeat Byzantine Emperor Constantine IV (681); first Bulgar-Slavic confederation established south of the Danube
Krum Khan defeats Byzantine army and kills Emperor Nikephoros I (811); Bulgaria extends to Adriatic and Aegean coasts; Preslav becomes capital
Boris I converts to Orthodox Christianity (864); Simeon I defeats Byzantium multiple times and titles himself 'Caesar of the Bulgarians and Romans'
Macedonian Byzantine dynasty's military revival; Basil II defeats Bulgaria at Kleidion (1014) and blinds 15,000 prisoners; Bulgaria absorbed into Byzantine Empire (1018)

rise_factors.description: Bulgar cavalry mobility combined with Slavic infantry to create a combined force that repeatedly defeated the heavier Byzantine professional army in Balkan terrain
Balkan mountain ranges, Stara Planina, Rhodopes, provided defensive depth against Byzantine campaigns from Constantinople

decline_factors.description: Byzantine Macedonian dynasty's military recovery under Nikephoros II and Basil II reversed Bulgar military advantage through superior organisation and siege technology

description: Buyid confederation of emirates (934–1062) founded by Daylamite warlords from the Caspian coast who captured Baghdad (945) and reduced the Abbasid caliph to a figurehead; as Shia rulers governing a Sunni caliph, the Buyids pioneered the Shia-Sunni administrative compromise that characterised many later Islamic dynasties, while their patronage of Arabic and Persian literature supported scholars including Avicenna and al-Biruni.

temporal.notes: Stub: dates from GeoJSON basemap years 1000–1200

lifecycle_phases.description: Buyid (Buwayhid) brothers conquered Persia from Daylamite highland base, seizing Baghdad in 945 and placing the Abbasid caliph under nominal rule.
Greatest territorial extent under Adud al-Dawla; major patronage of Persian literature, philosophy, and Shia scholarship.
Rival Buyid princes divided the empire; Seljuk pressure from the east steadily reduced territories.
Final Buyid ruler expelled from Baghdad by Seljuk Tughril Beg; dynasty ended.

rise_factors.description: Daylamite infantry were elite mountain fighters able to defeat Arab cavalry armies.
Buyids were Shia and used patronage of Shia shrines to build religious legitimacy in Iraq and Persia.
Abbasid caliphate's military collapse allowed Buyids to become kingmakers in Baghdad.

decline_factors.description: Buyid princes divided territories among sons, creating competing courts that fought each other.
Seljuk Turks overwhelmed Daylamite infantry with superior cavalry and numbers.

description: Continuation of the Eastern Roman Empire centered on Constantinople (330–1453) that preserved Roman law, Greek learning, and Chalcedonian Christianity through a millennium of adaptation; the primary buffer between Islam and Latin Europe, it transmitted classical heritage westward and shaped Orthodox civilisation across the Balkans and Russia before falling to the Ottomans.

temporal.notes: Continuous from Constantinople's founding; Latin interregnum 1204–1261

lifecycle_phases.description: Constantinople founded (330) as the new imperial capital; Justinian I (527–565) briefly reconquers Italy, North Africa, and southern Spain; Justinian's Plague (541) kills 25–50 million; Arab conquests strip Egypt, Syria, and Levant permanently

Theme (military district) system reorganizes defense; Basil II (976–1025) destroys the Bulgarian empire; empire reaches maximum medieval extent; Greek replaces Latin as the official language; Macedonian dynasty presides over cultural florescence

Seljuk defeat at Manzikert (1071) loses Anatolia; Komnenian emperors rebuild the army through pronoia (feudal grants); ally with Crusaders; Isaac II and Alexios III destabilize the dynasty; Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople (1204)

Nicaean Empire retakes Constantinople (1261); Palaiologos dynasty presides over a rump state; Black Death (1347) and Ottoman expansion reduce the empire to Constantinople and a few Aegean islands; final siege by Mehmed II ends the empire (1453)

rise_factors.description: Theme system reorganized provincial government around military districts, creating a self-financing defensive apparatus; Greek Orthodox Church provided ideological unity across diverse populations
Constantinople controlled the Bosphorus, the only crossing between Black Sea and Mediterranean; customs revenues from this chokepoint funded the empire for centuries
Constantinople's triple walls (Theodosian Walls) withstood 23 sieges over 1,000 years; the Golden Horn harbor gave naval advantages; the city was effectively impregnable to pre-gunpowder armies

Justinian I's Corpus Juris Civilis (529–534) codified Roman law in a form that shaped European legal systems for a millennium. Byzantine bureaucracy maintained this legal tradition through administrative continuity unavailable in successor states.

Greek fire, a liquid incendiary weapon projected from siphons that burned on water, gave the Byzantine navy a decisive technological advantage in sea battles. It repelled multiple Arab naval attacks (673–78, 717–18) that would otherwise have taken Constantinople.

Constantinople's control of the Bosphorus, the only passage between the Black Sea and Mediterranean, enabled toll collection on all maritime trade between the two seas. This geographic monopoly generated revenues supporting the empire through centuries of military decline.

Byzantine missionaries (Cyril and Methodius, 863) converted Slavic peoples to Orthodox Christianity while providing the Cyrillic alphabet, Greek-style governance, and Byzantine cultural models. This cultural export created a Byzantine Commonwealth of dependent states.

decline_factors.description: Byzantine political culture normalized coup attempts; soldiers' emperors and palace revolutions kept the state perpetually internally destabilized; civil wars of the 14th century (Andronikos II vs III, then John V vs John VI Kantakouzenos) invited Ottoman intervention

Fourth Crusade (1204) permanently fractured Byzantine power by sacking Constantinople and creating the Latin Empire; Seljuk defeat at Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement, removing the empire's core recruiting and revenue base

Plague of Justinian (541) killed 25–50 million across the empire, permanently reducing its tax base and military manpower during the most critical expansion phase. Black Death (1347) further devastated an already weakened population.

Grants of commercial privilege to Venice (1082), Genoa, and Pisa progressively outsourced Byzantine international trade to Italian merchants who paid no tolls. By the 12th century, Venetian merchants paid less tax than Byzantine subjects, a catastrophic fiscal erosion.

The theme system (military provinces whose soldier-farmers paid for their arms through land grants) was progressively undermined by great landowners absorbing peasant holdings. This eliminated the soldier-farmer class and forced reliance on expensive foreign mercenaries.

population_estimates.note: Peak resident population, among largest North American settlements.

description: Cahokia, located near modern St. Louis at the confluence of the Mississippi, Missouri, and Illinois rivers, was the largest pre-Columbian urban centre north of Mexico, peaking c.1100 with an estimated 10,000–20,000 inhabitants. The site centred on Monks Mound, a 30-metre-tall earthen pyramid that was the largest structure in North America until the late 19th century. Cahokia's Mississippian culture spread maize agriculture, shell-tempered ceramic technology, and the Southern Ceremonial Complex across the eastern woodlands. By c.1200 the site was already in decline; by c.1350 it was abandoned. Causes are debated: deforestation, Mississippi flooding, drought, political collapse, or some combination. Cahokia is the first Americas entity in this dataset.

internal_structure.legitimacy_basis: ceremonial authority of paramount chief; mound-builder cosmology
internal_structure.administrative_system: paramount chief over subordinate village mound centres

lifecycle_phases.description: Local Late Woodland populations consolidate around the future site.
Monks Mound, Grand Plaza, Woodhenge built; population peaks.
Stockades erected, population drops by 80%, finally abandoned.

rise_factors.description: Adoption of intensive maize agriculture supported dense populations along Mississippi bottomlands.
The Southern Ceremonial Complex centred ritual authority on Cahokia, attracting pilgrims and tribute.
Confluence of Mississippi, Missouri, and Illinois put Cahokia at the trade nexus of three river systems.

decline_factors.description: Clearance of bottomland forests for fuel and construction may have caused soil erosion and flooding.
Mid-13th-century drought (tree-ring-confirmed) likely reduced maize yields below sustainable levels.
Stockade defenses dating to c.1175 suggest growing internal violence; population dispersed.

secondary_bases: long-distance exchange of marine shell, copper, mica

description: Umayyad state in Iberia (929–1031) at its height the wealthiest and most literate polity in western Europe; the caliph Abd al-Rahman III's declaration of independent caliphate challenged Abbasid and Fatimid legitimacy while Córdoba's libraries, medicine, and philosophy catalysed the later twelfth-century translation movement that transformed European intellectual life.

temporal.notes: Proclaimed by Abd al-Rahman III; collapse leads to Taifa period

lifecycle_phases.description: Abd al-Rahman I, sole surviving Umayyad prince, escapes the Abbasid massacre and establishes an independent emirate in Iberia. Al-Andalus becomes a refuge for Umayyad culture; Córdoba grows into the largest city in Europe west of Constantinople.

Abd al-Rahman III proclaims a rival caliphate (929), challenging both the Abbasids in Baghdad and the Fatimids in Cairo. Al-Hakam II presides over a golden age of Islamic learning; Córdoba's library holds 400,000 volumes. Al-Mansur (981–1002) raids Santiago de Compostela, crushing Christian kingdoms.

Al-Mansur's death triggers civil war (fitna); Berber troops sack Córdoba's palace city of Medina Azahara (1010). The unified caliphate fragments into 30+ petty kingdoms (taifas), permanently ending Andalusian political unity.

rise_factors.description: As the last Umayyad dynasty, the Córdoba caliphate claimed authentic legitimacy against the Abbasid 'usurpers'; Abd al-Rahman III's assumption of the caliphal title challenged both Baghdad and the Fatimids

Al-Andalus controlled the western Mediterranean trade between the Islamic world and Christian Europe; Córdoba's market linked silk roads to Atlantic trade networks, making it the wealthiest city west of Baghdad

Sophisticated bureaucratic system based on Umayyad models, using both Arab and local Iberian administrative talent; efficient tax collection and agricultural management supported a large professional army

Córdoba under Abd al-Rahman III and al-Hakam II became Europe's largest city (perhaps 500,000 inhabitants) and its most intellectually advanced: its library held 400,000 volumes when the largest western European libraries held hundreds. Jewish, Christian, and Muslim scholars collaborated here.

Umayyad rulers introduced or expanded irrigation-dependent crops (rice, cotton, sugarcane, citrus, saffron) to Iberia, creating an agricultural revolution that made al-Andalus the most productive region in Europe and supported urban populations impossible elsewhere.

Abd al-Rahman III's assumption of the caliph title (929), rejecting both Abbasid and Fatimid authority, gave Córdoba full ideological independence and mobilized Andalusian Muslim identity around a local ruler claiming legitimate succession from the Prophet.

decline_factors.description: Al-Mansur's sons fought a civil war (fitna) that invited Berber mercenaries and Christian princes to interfere; the destruction of Medina Azahara (1010) symbolized the collapse of Umayyad prestige

The taifa fragmentation (post-1031) allowed Christian kingdoms to play competing Muslim princes against each other; Alfonso VI exploited taifa divisions to take Toledo (1085) without facing unified resistance

Chamberlain al-Mansur's (Almanzor) effective seizure of power under the child caliph Hisham II (r.976–1009) demonstrated fatal weakness: when Almanzor's sons competed to succeed him, they triggered a civil war (fitna) that shattered Umayyad legitimacy irreversibly.

The 1031 abolition of the Córdoban caliphate splintered al-Andalus into over 20 competing taifa kingdoms. These petty states were too small to resist Christian Reconquista pressure and frequently paid tribute to Christian kings rather than unite against them.

description: Frankish hegemony under Charlemagne and his successors (768–888) that forged the first political unity of western Europe since Rome; the imperial coronation of 800 reoriented papal-royal relations, its administrative system of counts and missi laid foundations for feudal governance, and its cultural renaissance in literacy and canon law shaped medieval civilisation for centuries.

temporal.notes: Frankish empire; ends with Treaty of Verdun

lifecycle_phases.description: Pippin III deposes the last Merovingian king (751) with papal approval. Charlemagne defeats the Lombards (774), conquers Saxony after 30-year campaigns, and defeats the Avars. Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800, the first Western Roman Emperor since 476. Carolingian Renaissance advances literacy and uniform administration.

Louis the Pious inherits an empire too large for a single ruler; his sons wage civil wars over inheritance. Battle of Fontenoy (841) proves the empire cannot be held together militarily. Treaty of Verdun (843) permanently partitions the empire into West Francia, East Francia, and Middle Francia.

rise_factors.description: Carolingian heavy cavalry and organized military aristocracy (knights with benefice grants) gave decisive tactical superiority over Umayyad cavalry at Tours (732), Lombard infantry, and Avar nomads. The missi dominici system coordinated military resources across vast territories.

Alliance between the Carolingian dynasty and the papacy gave the empire Christian imperial legitimacy; Charlemagne's coronation as emperor (800) linked Frankish power to the Roman imperial tradition and gave the pope a secular protector

County system, missi dominici (royal inspectors), and standardized coinage and weights created the most effective administrative apparatus in post-Roman Western Europe; the Carolingian Renaissance produced a trained literate clerical bureaucracy

Charles Martel's adoption of heavily armed cavalry (financed partly by secularized church lands) transformed Frankish warfare. Frankish heavy cavalry could defeat Arab, Saxon, and Avar infantry in open battle, giving the empire unmatched offensive power.

Charlemagne's missi dominici (imperial envoys sent in pairs, one layman, one cleric) traveled the empire conducting judicial inquiries, correcting abuses, and conveying royal commands. This itinerant bureaucracy extended central oversight to distant counties.

The Carolingian Renaissance revived Latin literacy, standardized the Carolingian minuscule script (ancestor of modern lowercase letters), established palace schools, and produced the majority of classical Latin manuscripts that survived to modernity.

Pope Leo III's coronation of Charlemagne as emperor (800 CE) created a Christian Roman Empire claim rivaling Byzantium. This papal-imperial alliance granted ideological legitimacy for Carolingian dominance that dynastic power alone could not provide.

decline_factors.description: Frankish inheritance custom divided kingdoms among all sons; Louis the Pious could not prevent his sons from fighting three civil wars over their shares. The Treaty of Verdun (843) made the east-west partition permanent, establishing the foundations of France and Germany.

Viking raids beginning 793 targeted undefended monasteries and river towns; Magyar cavalry raids penetrated deep into the Carolingian heartland from 900; Saracen raids threatened Mediterranean coasts. The empire had no standing navy and could not coordinate a defensive response.

The Treaty of Verdun (843) divided the empire among three grandsons: West Francia, Middle Francia, and East Francia. This partition was not intended as permanent but became so through subsequent treaty adjustments, ending unified Carolingian rule.

The 9th-century triple attack, Viking raids from the north, Saracen raids from the south, and Magyar cavalry raids from the east, overwhelmed the empire's defensive capacity simultaneously. Contemporaries saw the convergence as apocalyptic.

description: Mongol successor state in Central Asia (1226–1347) established by Chagatai Khan, second son of Genghis Khan; controlled the heartland of Transoxiana and the Tarim Basin; internal conflict between nomadic and settled factions led to its fragmentation and eventual replacement by the Timurid Empire.

temporal.notes: Founded by Chagatai Khan; split into eastern (Moghulistan) and western (Transoxiana) halves c.1334; western half conquered by Timur by 1370

lifecycle_phases.description: Chagatai Khan rules as loyal subordinate to the Great Khan; administers Central Asian heartland; court maintains nomadic traditions while administering settled Transoxiana through Persian bureaucrats
Khanate divided between pro-nomadic factions favoring Mongolian steppe lifestyle and pro-settled factions seeking to embrace Persian-Islamic civilization; persistent succession wars
Khan Kebek builds permanent capital at Qarshi; monetary reforms; partial Islamization; eastern territories remain nomadic; Black Death and Timur's rise end Chagatai power

rise_factors.description: Chagatai's status as son of Genghis Khan gave the khanate unquestioned legitimacy among Mongol tribes; the Silk Road heartland was the wealthiest inheritance in the Mongol partition
Control of Transoxiana and the Tarim Basin gave the Chagatai Khanate revenues from the most trafficked section of the overland Silk Road connecting China to the Middle East
Positioned between the Ilkhanate, Golden Horde, and Yuan Dynasty, Chagatai khans could play rivals against each other and extract concessions from all three

decline_factors.description: Fundamental tension between nomadic Mongol identity and the need to govern settled Persian-speaking cities produced repeated civil wars that prevented stable institutions
Timur (Tamerlane), a Barlas Turco-Mongol from Transoxiana, progressively absorbed Chagatai territory from 1360 onward, culminating in control of all former Chagatai lands by 1380
The plague devastated trade-dependent Central Asian cities in the 1340s, collapsing the Silk Road revenues that sustained the khanate

description: Deccan-based dynasty (543–753 CE, Western Chalukyas) that dominated the Indian peninsula from the Narmada to the Kaveri; the Badami Chalukyas checked northward Harsha expansion and southward Pallava pressure, pioneering the Vesara architectural style in cave temples and structural monuments at Aihole, Badami, and Pattadakal that influenced all subsequent Deccan temple architecture.

lifecycle_phases.description: Chalukya kingdom emerged in the Deccan under Pulakesi I; expanded to dominate the central peninsula.
Pulakesi II repelled Harsha's invasion from the north and established Chalukya supremacy; defeated by Pallavas in 642.
Dynasty recovered under Vikramaditya I but never regained full power; overthrown by the Rashtrakutas in 753.
Western Chalukya branch (Chalukyas of Kalyani) restored Deccan power after Rashtrakuta decline.

rise_factors.description: Chalukya war elephants and integrated cavalry-infantry formations made them formidable against northern armies.
The Deccan plateau provided a defensible base from which to project power north and south.
Patronage of Hindu and Jain temples built religious legitimacy and artisan networks.

decline_factors.description: Repeated costly wars with Pallava dynasty drained military resources.
Internal revolt by Dantidurga established the Rashtrakuta dynasty in place of the Chalukyas (753).

description: Indianised coastal kingdom of central Vietnam (192–1832) whose Hindu and later Muslim rulers competed with the Vietnamese Đại Việt for control of the Indochinese coast; Cham sailors dominated South China Sea trade and Cham sculptural tradition, visible in the My Son sanctuary, represents the finest Hindu monumental art of mainland Southeast Asia; gradual Vietnamese southward expansion ultimately absorbed Cham territory.

lifecycle_phases.description: Cham kingdom of Lâm Ấp emerges from Chinese collapse in the south; Indianised court culture adopted; Hindu temple construction begins
Multiple Cham kingdoms, Panduranga, Kauthara, Amaravati, control central Vietnamese coast; My Son sanctuary at height; maritime trade flourishing
Vietnamese Đại Việt advance southward; Cham sacks Hanoi (1371) but cannot prevent Vietnamese colonisation; Vijaya capital taken (1471)
Champa reduced to rump state in Panduranga; slow Vietnamese absorption; final sultanate extinguished

rise_factors.description: Cham ports controlled the coastal trade route between the South China Sea and the Gulf of Thailand, collecting duties from East-West maritime traffic

decline_factors.description: Vietnamese demographic and agricultural expansion down the coast could not be reversed by Cham military resistance; slow attrition defeated Cham political autonomy

description: Rajput dynasty of the Chahamanas of Shakambhari (c. 6th–12th c.) controlling Rajputana and the Delhi region; Prithviraj III's defeat at the Second Battle of Tarain (1192) by Muhammad of Ghor ended Rajput military dominance of northern India and opened the subcontinent to the Delhi Sultanate; Prithviraj's romantic legend and Chand Bardai's Prithvirajraso epic made him the paradigmatic Rajput warrior-king in Indian historical memory.

lifecycle_phases.description: Chahamana (Chauhan) dynasty rose in Rajputana from a subordinate lineage to control Shakambhari and surrounding territory.
Expanded control over Ajmer and Dilli; became dominant Rajput power of northern India.
Prithviraj III represented peak Chauhan power; resisted Muhammad of Ghor at First Battle of Tarain (1191) but was defeated at Second Battle (1192).
Ghurid conquest destroyed Chauhan power; dynasty fragmented into small principalities.

rise_factors.description: Chauhan cavalry was among the finest in Rajputana; tradition of warfare maintained battle-hardened nobility.
Control of Ajmer and Delhi region gave access to the Gangetic plain's wealth.

decline_factors.description: Defeat at the Second Battle of Tarain (1192) by Muhammad of Ghor was decisive and irreversible.
Rajput kingdoms failed to form a united front against the Ghurid invasion.

religion: Hindu Shaivism with significant Mahayana Buddhist presence

population_estimates.note: Tonle Sap floodplain peak.

description: Chenla (c.550–802) is the conventional Chinese-source name for the pre-Angkor Khmer kingdom that succeeded Funan in the Mekong basin. Chenla's capital at Sambor Prei Kuk preserved Funan's Indianised court culture but shifted the political centre inland, away from maritime trade and toward an agricultural base centred on Tonle Sap fishing and rice terracing. The kingdom fragmented in the 8th century into 'Land Chenla' (north) and 'Water Chenla' (south), which were reunified by Jayavarman II in 802, the conventional foundation date of the Khmer Empire of Angkor.

lifecycle_phases.description: Chenla absorbs Funanese territory under Bhavavarman I.
Sambor Prei Kuk becomes the largest pre-Angkor temple complex.
Split into Land/Water Chenla; reunified by Jayavarman II in 802 as Khmer Empire.

rise_factors.description: Chenla kings claimed Funanese royal lineage to legitimise inland expansion.
Tonle Sap floodplain rice agriculture provided a stable surplus distinct from Funan's maritime base.
Adoption of the cult of Shiva-Linga grounded royal legitimacy in Indic kingship.

decline_factors.description: Late-7th-century split into 'Land Chenla' and 'Water Chenla' weakened the polity.
Javanese (Srivijayan / Shailendra) raids on coastal Water Chenla disrupted southern administration.

key_figures.name: Bhavavarman I
key_figures.notes: Founder of Chenla via marriage to Funan princess.

key_figures.name: Isanavarman I
key_figures.notes: Built Sambor Prei Kuk capital.

key_figures.name: Jayavarman II
key_figures.notes: Reunified Chenla and proclaimed himself chakravartin in 802, founding Angkor.

population_estimates.note: Chan Chan resident population estimate; total kingdom likely ~600,000.

description: Late-Intermediate Period kingdom occupying the north coast of present-day Peru, with its capital at Chan Chan, a planned earthen-walled city of some twelve square kilometres, the largest pre-Columbian urban centre in the Americas before Tenochtitlan. Chimor's coastal-irrigation polity controlled a thousand-kilometre stretch from Tumbes south to the Lima area until the late-fifteenth-century Inca conquest under Tupac Inca Yupanqui absorbed it into Tawantinsuyu.

temporal.notes: North-coast Peruvian kingdom centred on Chan Chan; absorbed by the Inca conquest under Tupac Inca Yupanqui around 1470.

geographic.notes: Centroid set at Chan Chan near modern Trujillo.

lifecycle_phases.description: Early Chimor consolidation around Chan Chan after collapse of Moche.
Hydraulic expansion across north-coast valleys; Chan Chan reaches monumental form.
Late Chimor reaches Tumbes in the north; Inca conquest c. 1470 ends independent rule.

rise_factors.description: Engineered canals linking the Moche, Chicama, and Jequetepeque valleys irrigated tens of thousands of hectares of coastal desert.
Ciudadela compound system, each king built a new walled palace, sealed at death, gave continuity to a dynastic-administrative apparatus.

decline_factors.description: Topa Inca Yupanqui's c. 1470 conquest absorbed Chimor into Tawantinsuyu, ending independent rule.

sources.title: The Incas

description: South Indian maritime empire (c. 850–1279) under the imperial Chola dynasty that conquered Sri Lanka, the Malabar coast, and launched naval expeditions to Southeast Asia (1025) reaching Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula, and the Bay of Bengal coasts; the Chola bronze tradition, the Nataraja dancing Shiva, represents the highest achievement of medieval Indian bronzework, while their hydraulic infrastructure in the Kaveri delta supported the most productive agricultural system in medieval South Asia.

lifecycle_phases.description: Early Chola dynasty dominated parts of Tamil Nadu; mentioned in Sangam literature as patrons of Tamil poetry.
Medieval Chola revival under Vijayalaya; recaptured Tanjore from Pandyas and re-established the dynasty.
Rajaraja I and Rajendra I created a maritime empire stretching from Sri Lanka to Sumatra; navy raided Srivijaya.
Gradually lost northern territories to Hoysalas and Pandyas; final rulers were subordinate to Pandya overlords.

rise_factors.description: Chola navy was the most powerful in the Indian Ocean; enabled Sri Lanka conquest and Srivijaya raids.
Village-level sabha councils and inscribed temple records created an unusually well-documented administrative system.
Major temples served as banks, granaries, and economic centres that stabilised regional commerce.

decline_factors.description: Pandya kingdom systematically eroded Chola power in the 13th century, culminating in conquest of Tanjore.
Later Chola kings were increasingly subordinate clients of rival dynasties.

description: Finno-Ugric peoples (medieval term used by Slavic chroniclers for eastern Finnic groups including Estonians, Veps, and related tribes) who inhabited the forest zone between the Baltic and the Urals; incorporated into Novgorodian commercial networks as fur tribute-payers, the Chuds resisted Christianisation longer than Baltic neighbors and appear in Russian chronicles as opponents of Novgorodian and Livonian expansion into the Baltic-Finnish forest zone.

lifecycle_phases.description: Finnic-speaking Chuds (proto-Estonians) inhabited the eastern Baltic and Ladoga region; semi-nomadic with fishing and fur-trade economy.
Chuds featured in the Varangian origin story (Rurik's invitation); integrated into early Russian trade networks.
Gradually absorbed into Russian and German (Livonian) spheres; distinct Chud identity disappeared from historical sources.

description: Italian city-commune (c. 1097–1395) that pioneered consular self-government against episcopal and imperial authority; its resistance to Frederick Barbarossa through the Lombard League secured the Peace of Constance (1183) establishing communal autonomy as a constitutional norm in northern Italy, before eventual signorial transformation under the Visconti.

temporal.notes: Communal phase; Lombard League against Barbarossa

lifecycle_phases.description: Milan declares itself a commune (1097), one of the first Italian cities to achieve self-governance against the authority of the Archbishop and Holy Roman Emperor. It leads the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa, whose destruction of Milan (1162) galvanizes Italian city resistance; the League defeats him at Legnano (1176), the first great victory of infantry over feudal cavalry. Milan becomes the most populous city in medieval Europe north of Rome.

The Visconti family defeats the Della Torre family (1277) and establishes hereditary signorial rule while maintaining communal forms. Gian Galeazzo Visconti (1378–1402) consolidates the signoria, purchases the title of Duke of Milan (1395) from Emperor Wenceslaus IV, and nearly creates a unified northern Italian state before dying of plague. The commune is effectively over; the Duchy of Milan succeeds it.

rise_factors.description: Milan's position at the foot of the Alpine passes made it the distribution hub for trans-Alpine trade; Milanese wool, silk, and armor industries supplied markets from England to the Ottoman Empire, funding the civic programs and military ambitions of the commune

The Lombard League's innovation at Legnano (1176), using the carroccio (sacred war wagon) as a rallying point for infantry in a mixed formation against feudal cavalry, demonstrated that disciplined communal infantry could defeat armored knights

Milan led the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa, demonstrating its capacity to mobilize north Italian cities in coalition; defeating the emperor at Legnano (1176) established Milan as the preeminent communal power in Lombardy

Milan's control of the upper Po plain gave it access to the most productive agricultural land in Italy; surplus grain funded the Visconti and Sforza courts and supported a dense urban artisan population

Milanese armor and weapons workshops supplied armies across Europe by the 14th century; the city's metallurgical expertise, fed by Alpine iron, created an export industry that funded political ambitions and attracted skilled workers

Milan's commune wrested self-governance from the Archbishop through the Credenza di Sant'Ambrogio in 1198, establishing elected consuls who managed taxation, justice, and military conscription independent of imperial or episcopal authority.

decline_factors.description: Factional conflict between the Guelph Della Torre and Ghibelline Visconti families consumed Milanese politics for decades; the commune's republican institutions could not resolve these conflicts, enabling the Visconti to establish permanent signorial power

The struggle between the Torriani and Visconti families in the late 13th century exemplified the vulnerability of communal institutions to aristocratic capture; the commune's elected consuls could not resist signorie who combined wealth and military force

Every imperial expedition (Henry VII 1310, Louis IV 1327) disrupted Milanese political stability; the city oscillated between Guelph and Ghibelline alignments depending on which external power threatened most, preventing the emergence of stable institutions

Recurrent factional violence between the Guelph Della Torre and Ghibelline Visconti families destabilized communal governance; the Visconti signoria established in 1277 ended the commune's republican institutions and concentrated power in a single dynasty.

lifecycle_phases.description: Corsica passed between Byzantine, Lombard, and Saracen control; frequent Arab raids devastated coastal settlements.
Charlemagne incorporated Corsica; Frankish control was nominal and local lords effectively self-governing.
Genoa and Pisa competed for Corsica; Genoa ultimately prevailed and established colonial administration.

rise_factors.description: Central position in the western Mediterranean made Corsica strategically valuable for any maritime power.

decline_factors.description: Corsica's strategic value always attracted external powers; the island never developed sufficient internal cohesion for independence.
Recurrent Saracen raids in the 8th-10th centuries destroyed coastal settlements and fragmented political authority.

description: Strategically pivotal county astride the Loire (c. 870–1204) whose counts steadily accumulated Touraine, Maine, and eventually England through marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine; the Angevin inheritance assembled a cross-Channel empire that put the French crown under existential pressure until Philip II dismantled it by conquering Normandy and Anjou in 1204.

temporal.notes: Plantagenet dynastic base; c.870 formation approximate.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Ingelger and Fulk the Red establish the comital dynasty on the Loire.
Fulk Nerra builds the castle network; Angevin expansion into Touraine and Maine.
Geoffrey Plantagenet acquires Normandy; Anjou becomes the core of an Atlantic empire.
Angevin empire maintained as English possession; French pressure mounts.
Philip II Augustus conquers Anjou; incorporated into the French royal domain.

rise_factors.description: Strategic marriages accumulated Maine, Touraine, and ultimately Normandy through the 11th–12th centuries.
Fulk Nerra built a network of frontier castles creating defensible buffer zones against rivals.
Consistent transmission to capable heirs through four generations produced institutional continuity.

Anjou controlled the middle Loire, the main route between Atlantic commerce and Parisian markets. The Loire wines produced in the county's heartland and toll revenues from Loire river traffic funded Angevin military ambitions.

Henry II's accession to the English throne (1154) transformed Anjou from a regional county into the senior partner in the Angevin Empire stretching from Scotland to the Pyrenees. Angevin resources, English royal revenues plus French territories, made Henry the most powerful western European ruler.

Successive counts of Anjou pursued strategic marriages and military campaigns to absorb Maine (1110) and Normandy (1144), assembling the territorial bloc that gave their dynasty claim to the English throne.

decline_factors.description: Philip II Augustus systematically captured Normandy, Maine, and Anjou 1202–1204.
Rivalry between John and Arthur of Brittany delegitimized the Angevin claim to French support.
French royal conquest eliminated Anjou as an independent political unit.

Philip II Augustus's conquest of Anjou (1204), along with Normandy and other Angevin territories, ended Anjou's independent political significance. The county was absorbed directly into the French royal domain, its resources redirected to Capetian rather than Angevin ambitions.

description: Frankish march county (801–1162) that gradually shed Carolingian suzerainty while expanding south into al-Andalus; its union with the Crown of Aragon through Ramon Berenguer IV's marriage to Petronilla of Aragon (1137) created the composite Aragonese-Catalan federation that dominated the western Mediterranean for two centuries.

temporal.notes: Catalan dynasty merged with Aragon under Ramon Berenguer IV

lifecycle_phases.description: Charlemagne's forces capture Barcelona (801) from the Umayyads, establishing it as the capital of the Spanish March, a Frankish frontier zone. The counts of Barcelona hold the position under Frankish suzerainty; Guifré el Pilós (the Hairy, 878–897) becomes the first hereditary count of Barcelona, founding the Catalan dynasty. The counts increasingly act independently as Carolingian power collapses.

Count Borrell II refuses to recognize Hugh Capet as king (988), effectively making Catalonia independent of France. The counts expand south through the Reconquista, capturing Tarragona and the lower Ebro. Ramon Berenguer III (1082–1131) marries the heiress of Provence, extending Catalan control into southern France. His son Ramon Berenguer IV marries the heiress of Aragon (1137), creating the Crown of Aragon.

rise_factors.description: Barcelona's Mediterranean port gave Catalonia access to the trade networks of the western Mediterranean; combined with Provence (after 1112), the county controlled the coastal routes from the Rhône to the Ebro, positioning it to become the commercial heart of the Crown of Aragon

Barcelona's merchants created a Mediterranean commercial network rivaling Genoa; the Llibre del consolat de mar (c. 1272) codified maritime commercial law adopted across the Mediterranean; Catalan trading colonies in Sicily, Sardinia, and Greece generated wealth channeled through Barcelona

Barcelona's harbor gave the county direct access to Mediterranean trade. Catalan merchants became dominant in western Mediterranean commerce (Genoa-Pisa competition zone), establishing trading posts from Sardinia to Sicily.

The marriage of Ramon Berenguer IV to Petronilla of Aragon (1137) united the county with Aragon's territory. This dynastic union created the Crown of Aragon, with Barcelona providing commercial-maritime resources and Aragon providing territorial depth.

Barcelona originated as a Carolingian frontier march established to defend against Moorish raids. This military origin gave its counts institutional independence: they developed their own administration without strong royal oversight.
The Usatges de Barcelona (c.1060), one of Europe's earliest feudal law codes, codified rights and obligations, reducing arbitrary lordship and attracting settlers to Catalan frontier expansion zones.

Established as a Carolingian march against the Umayyads around 801, Barcelona's counts gradually became independent as Carolingian power collapsed, with Wifred the Hairy refusing to pay homage in 878 and founding the hereditary Catalan comital dynasty.

decline_factors.description: Ramon Berenguer IV's marriage to Petronilla of Aragon (1137) merged the county into the larger Crown of Aragon; the county's identity was preserved but its independent political significance ended as Aragon's military weight dominated the combined state

The union of Aragon and Barcelona under Ramón Berenguer IV (1137) gradually subordinated the county's identity within the larger Crown of Aragon; Castilian dominance after 1479 further marginalized the Catalan commercial tradition

After the union with Aragon, Barcelona gradually lost political autonomy. Aragonese territorial policy often conflicted with Catalan commercial interests; repeated feudal conflicts between Catalan cities and the crown eroded the county's independent standing.
