description: Goryeo kingdom (918–1392) that unified the Korean peninsula and gave Korea its name; under the Wang dynasty, Goryeo developed the world's first moveable metal type (1230s), sponsored Mahayana Buddhist art and the Tripitaka Koreana woodblock scripture collection, and maintained sophisticated diplomatic relations with Song, Liao, Jin, and Mongol dynasties; Mongol invasions (1231–1270) forced submission but preserved the dynasty as a client state.

lifecycle_phases.description: Wang Geon (Taejo) unifies Later Three Kingdoms; Goryeo capital at Kaesong; Buddhism established as state religion
Gwangjong's civil service examinations; Buddhist Tripitaka woodblock printing; celadon pottery achieves world-class refinement; population 2+ million
Military coup (1170) establishes Choe clan dictatorship; three Mongol invasions (1231, 1235, 1254); Tripitaka Koreana burned and remade
Goryeo becomes Mongol vassal state; yuan-controlled kings intermarry with Mongol princesses; tributary system extracts resources; Red Turban invasions
Yi Seonggye's coup; Goryeo replaced by Joseon dynasty at Hanyang (Seoul)

rise_factors.description: Wang Geon's policy of incorporating former Silla aristocracy and Later Baekje leadership maintained elite buy-in during unification
State Buddhism provided ideological unity and educated monastic administrators who staffed both temples and government offices

decline_factors.description: Mongol invasions destroyed agricultural infrastructure across the Korean peninsula and imposed a tributary relationship that drained both population and resources

description: Baltic tribal confederation (Couronians) of the eastern Baltic coast who were skilled seafarers and raiders active in Scandinavia, Ireland, and the Russian river systems in the Viking Age; the Teutonic Order's Northern Crusades (13th c.) converted and subjugated the Couronians, whose territory became the Duchy of Courland and whose distinct cultural identity merged into Latvian identity during the Baltic national awakening.

temporal.notes: Baltic Couronians active until the Livonian Order completed their conquest in 1267.

geographic.no_central_capital_reason: Baltic tribal confederation along the Curonian coast.

lifecycle_phases.description: Couronians (Kurs) inhabited the Curonian coast of Latvia; skilled seafarers and raiders who attacked Scandinavian coastal settlements.
Livonian Order systematically conquered Courland during the Northern Crusades; Couronians submitted by 1267.
Assimilated into the Livonian Confederation as a subordinate Baltic people under German lordship.

rise_factors.description: Curonian seafarers were formidable raiders who regularly attacked Scandinavian and Danish coasts.
Baltic amber from the Curonian coast was a high-value export commodity.

decline_factors.description: Livonian Order's crusading army with castle-building capacity overwhelmed Curonian tribal resistance.

description: Arab kingdom of the Banu Lakhm, ruling from the city of al-Hira on the lower Euphrates as a client of the Sasanian Persian empire. The Lakhmids fielded auxiliary cavalry on the Persian side of the long Roman-Persian wars and competed with the Byzantine-aligned Ghassanids across the Syrian Desert. Their deposition by Khusrau II in 602 deprived the Sasanians of an Arab buffer state and is sometimes cited as a contributing factor to the early Islamic conquest of Mesopotamia a generation later.

temporal.notes: Arab client kingdom of the Sasanian Persians centred on al-Hira on the lower Euphrates; deposed by the Sasanian king Khusrau II in 602, after which the Sasanians administered the frontier directly.

geographic.notes: Capital al-Hira on the lower Euphrates south of Kufa; the polity controlled tribal-bedouin frontiers between Sasanian Mesopotamia and inland Arabia.

description: Latin feudal empire established at Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade (1204–1261) that proved incapable of consolidating control over Byzantine territories; its French-dominated feudal structure was ill-suited to administering a complex urban empire, its perpetual financial crises forced pawning of Constantinople's greatest relics, and its reconquest by Nicaea was merely a matter of time.

temporal.notes: Crusader state on Byzantine ruins; reconquered by Michael VIII

lifecycle_phases.description: The Fourth Crusade, diverted by Venetian commercial interests and internal Byzantine politics, sacks Constantinople (April 1204), the greatest Christian city in the world. Baldwin of Flanders becomes the first Latin Emperor. The crusaders divide the Byzantine Empire: Venice takes the key islands and ports (three-eighths), while Frankish nobles carve out Greece into principalities. The Latin Empire controls Constantinople and Thrace but is immediately surrounded by hostile Greek successor states.

The Latin Empire never controls more than a fraction of the former Byzantine territory. The Greek Despotate of Epirus and Empire of Nicaea contest the remaining territory. Emperor Baldwin II (1228–1261) is so impoverished he pawns the Crown of Thorns to Venetian merchants. Michael VIII Palaiologos of Nicaea retakes Constantinople (1261) with Genoese naval support, ending the Latin Empire and restoring Byzantium.

rise_factors.description: The combined Venetian naval power and Crusader heavy cavalry made the Fourth Crusade force able to storm the walls of Constantinople, something no force had accomplished in 900 years; the Venetian fleet's mastery of the Golden Horn was decisive

The sack of Constantinople (1204) was one of the most spectacular military windfalls in medieval history; the accumulated wealth of the Byzantine capital, relics, gold, silk, manuscripts, funded the initial Crusader state and provided the prestige that attracted further western settlers

Venice's treaty rights from 1204 gave it three-eighths of Constantinople and preferential trading rights throughout the empire; Venetian commercial infrastructure, the fleet, the counting houses, the factors in every port, gave the Latin Empire an economic backbone that pure military conquest could not have provided

The Partitio Romaniae divided Byzantine territory among crusading nobles; French lords in the Duchy of Athens and the Principality of Achaea established functioning feudal states that outlasted the Latin Empire itself, demonstrating that western feudal institutions could transplant to Greek soil

Baldwin I's coronation as Latin Emperor in Hagia Sophia in 1204 briefly realized the dream of a Catholic-governed Constantinople, granting western crusaders access to the city's legendary wealth and commercial position.

decline_factors.description: The Latin Empire never gained legitimacy in the eyes of the Greek Orthodox population; the sacking of churches, removal of relics, and installation of Latin clergy in Orthodox sees created permanent hostility from the majority population

The Latin Empire held only Constantinople and fragments of Thrace while simultaneously claiming sovereignty over all former Byzantine territories; the impossibility of holding this position with the available manpower, mostly Italian merchant soldiers rather than traditional Crusader knights, made collapse inevitable

The Latin emperors never won the loyalty of the Greek-speaking majority; Orthodox clergy refused communion with the Latin hierarchy, peasants withheld taxes, and Greek nobles fled to Nicaea or Trebizond where Byzantine legitimacy was preserved

The Empire of Nicaea under the Laskaris dynasty preserved Byzantine military institutions and steadily reconquered territory; the Latin Empire was always on the defensive, losing its Anatolian and Thracian territories incrementally before Constantinople fell to Michael VIII in 1261

Michael VIII Palaiologos's forces recaptured Constantinople in 1261 by exploiting a moment when the Latin fleet was away; the last Latin emperor Baldwin II fled into exile, ending the 57-year experiment in Latin rule.

description: Khitan dynasty (907–1125) that built the first steppe empire to successfully govern both nomadic and sedentary populations using a dual administrative system; controlling northern China and Mongolia from their Shangjing capital, the Liao established diplomatic equality with the Song through the Chanyuan Treaty (1005) and extracted annual tribute, while Khitan script, art, and Buddhism developed a distinctive northern Chinese frontier civilisation.

lifecycle_phases.description: Yelü Abaoji unifies Khitan tribes; captures Sixteen Prefectures from Later Jin (947); dual administrative system established
Chanyuan Treaty (1005) with Song: 120,000 bolts of silk and 200,000 oz silver annual tribute; Liao controls northern steppe and border Chinese territories
Succession conflicts; Jurchen Wanyan clan in Manchuria resists Liao authority
Jurchen Jin dynasty wars; Song alliance abandons Chanyuan arrangement; Liao emperor captured; Kara-Khitan western remnant survives until 1218

rise_factors.description: Liao's Northern and Southern Court system, separate administrations for Khitan nomads and sedentary Chinese, successfully governed both populations without forcing either to adopt the other's lifestyle
Khitan cavalry mobility gave Liao military projection across both steppe and agricultural frontier zones inaccessible to Song infantry

decline_factors.description: Late Liao succession disputes weakened central authority precisely when Jurchen Jin military power was developing in Manchuria

description: Crusading military order state in the eastern Baltic (1237–1561) combining the Sword Brothers with the Teutonic Order; it Christianised and colonised the Baltic peoples of modern Latvia and Estonia through systematic conquest and settlement, creating a German-speaking noble colonist class whose legacy shaped Baltic social structure into the twentieth century.

temporal.notes: Northern crusader state; merger of Sword Brothers and Teutonic Order

lifecycle_phases.description: The Livonian Order (a branch of the Teutonic Order) conquers the pagan Latvian and Estonian tribes through the Northern Crusades. The order rules as a military theocracy with the Archbishop of Riga. Alexander Nevsky's victory at Lake Peipus (1242), the 'Battle on the Ice', halts the Order's eastward expansion at the Russian border.

The Livonian Order purchases Estonia from Denmark (1346). The state prospers through Baltic trade, Riga is a major Hanseatic city. The Order competes with the Archbishop of Riga for control of the ecclesiastical state, leading to endemic internal conflict. Growing Lithuanian-Polish pressure and the reformation of the Teutonic Order's Prussian state (1466) isolate Livonia. The 16th century brings Russian aggression under Ivan the Terrible.

rise_factors.description: The Livonian crusade ideology, converting pagan Balts and Finns, attracted Western European knights and funding for two centuries; papal support legitimized the Order's military campaigns as Christian missions

Riga's position on the Daugava river gave the Livonian Order control of the main route from the Baltic to the Russian interior; Hanseatic membership made Riga one of the most important commercial cities in northern Europe

The Livonian Brothers of the Sword (and later the Teutonic Order's Livonian branch) operated under a permanent papal crusading bull that justified military conquest and conversion; this mandate attracted German knights and settlers who formed the ruling class of the Livonian state

Riga (founded 1201) became a major Hanseatic city that channeled eastern Baltic trade, amber, furs, wax, timber, to western markets; the commercial revenues funded the Order's castles and supported an urban merchant class that gave the state economic depth beyond agricultural extraction

The Livonian Order built a dense network of stone castles across the eastern Baltic; these fortifications enabled small garrisons to control large hinterlands and withstand sieges by Lithuanian or Russian armies that lacked siege engineering

The Livonian Brothers of the Sword and their successors the Livonian Order used crusading ideology to justify conquest and conversion of Estonian and Latvian peoples, building fortified towns and bishoprics along the Daugava and Gauja rivers.

decline_factors.description: The permanent conflict between the Livonian Order and the Archbishop of Riga for control of the ecclesiastical state prevented unified resistance to external threats; the two powers repeatedly sought outside support (papacy, Empire, Lithuania) that further complicated governance

The defeat at Grunwald (1410) broke Teutonic Order power in Prussia; though Livonia was separate, the psychological blow, the loss of Prussian revenues, and the disruption of German recruitment networks weakened the Livonian branch that depended on the same institutions

The Protestant Reformation spread rapidly through Livonian merchant cities in the 1520s; the resulting religious conflict between Protestant burghers and the Catholic Order undermined the Order's authority and cohesion, leaving it unable to coordinate defense against Russian expansion under Ivan IV

Though Grunwald (1410) primarily destroyed the Teutonic Order proper, the Livonian Order's subsequent weakening by wars with Lithuania and Novgorod culminated in dissolution during the Livonian War (1558–83) against Ivan the Terrible.

description: Northern Italian kingdom established by Germanic Lombard migrants (568–774) that permanently reshaped the peninsula's ethnic and political landscape; its conquest of Byzantine exarchates threatened papal independence, making the Lombard threat the direct cause of the papacy's Carolingian alliance, the defeat of the Lombard kingdom, and ultimately the transfer of central Italy to Frankish and later German imperial jurisdiction.

temporal.notes: Conquered by Charlemagne 774; southern duchies persist

lifecycle_phases.description: The Lombards under King Alboin invade northern Italy (568), exploiting Byzantine exhaustion after the Gothic Wars. They rapidly overrun the Po Valley (Lombardy) and establish a kingdom at Pavia. Italy is carved between the Lombards (north and center), the Byzantines (Ravenna, Rome, Naples, Sicily), and the papacy (Rome). Alboin is assassinated (572); the kingdom briefly fragments among regional dukes.

King Agilulf (590–616) restores unity and secures peace with Byzantium. The Edict of Rothari (643) is the first written Lombard law code in Latin. The conversion from Arianism to Catholicism under Grimoald (662–671) removes the religious barrier between Lombards and the Italian population. The kingdom reaches its greatest extent under Liutprand (712–744) who nearly conquers Rome and the exarchate of Ravenna.

Liutprand's aggression against the papacy leads to papal appeals to the Franks. Pippin III intervenes (754, 756) but does not destroy the kingdom. His son Charlemagne invades (773), besieges Pavia, and deposes King Desiderius (774), incorporating the Lombard Kingdom into the Carolingian Empire. Charlemagne takes the title 'King of the Franks and Lombards.'

rise_factors.description: The Byzantine Empire was exhausted by decades of Gothic Wars (535–554) when the Lombards invaded; the exarchs in Ravenna lacked the resources to expel the newcomers, allowing the kingdom to consolidate in the Po Valley
The Edict of Rothari (643) systematically codified Lombard customary law in Latin, integrating Roman legal traditions and providing a uniform legal framework across the kingdom

The Lombard invasion of Italy (568) exploited Byzantine overstretching after the Gothic Wars. Lombard warrior-aristocrats secured the fertile Po Valley within three years, establishing a permanent territorial base.

Lombard artisans excelled in metalwork, particularly sword-making at Brescia and Bergamo. This craft specialization built guild structures that survived the kingdom's fall and contributed to Northern Italian commercial prosperity.

The Lombard invasion of Italy in 568 under Alboin swept over a Byzantine-ravaged peninsula still recovering from the Gothic Wars, meeting minimal resistance and establishing a kingdom within months that lasted two centuries.

decline_factors.description: Charlemagne's Frankish heavy cavalry and siege capabilities overwhelmed Lombard defenses; the fall of Pavia (774) after a six-month siege ended the kingdom

Lombard aggression against the papacy (especially Liutprand's campaigns 720s–740s) turned the spiritual authority of the Latin Church against the kingdom; papal appeals to the Franks provided the ideological justification for Carolingian intervention

Charlemagne's invasion (773–774) at papal invitation destroyed the Lombard kingdom in a single campaign. Desiderius surrendered Pavia after a siege; Charlemagne took the iron crown and declared himself "King of the Lombards."

Pope Stephen II's Donation of Pepin (754) created a Franco-papal alliance specifically against Lombard expansion. This alliance gave the papacy military backing that permanently constrained Lombard Italian hegemony.

Charlemagne's conquest at the invitation of Pope Hadrian I in 773–774 ended the Lombard kingdom; Charlemagne adopted the Iron Crown of Lombardy and incorporated the northern Italian territories into the Frankish empire.

description: Anglo-Norman and English lordship (1171–1541) established by Henry II's expedition; its actual control rarely extended beyond the Pale around Dublin, while successive English absentee lords and native Irish resistance produced the 'degenerate English' phenomenon, colonists who culturally assimilated to Gaelic ways, making Ireland a perpetual drain on English resources and a source of constitutional innovation in the concept of overseas lordship.

temporal.notes: Anglo-Norman lordship under English crown

lifecycle_phases.description: Henry II of England declares himself Lord of Ireland (1171–1172), following the Norman mercenary invasion invited by Dermot MacMurrough. His son John (later King John) is made Lord of Ireland (1177). Anglo-Norman lords (de Clare, de Burgh, le Gros) carve out substantial lordships while Gaelic Irish kings survive in the west and north. The Statutes of Kilkenny (1366) later attempt to prevent Anglo-Norman assimilation into Irish culture.

The Anglo-Norman settlement contracts to the 'Pale' around Dublin and a few coastal towns as Gaelic Ireland reasserts itself. The Bruce invasion (1315–1318) briefly threatens English control. By 1500, the Earl of Kildare (Fitzgerald family) runs Ireland as a de facto autonomous lord, barely acknowledging English authority. The 'mere English' become 'more Irish than the Irish themselves.'

rise_factors.description: Norman castle-building and heavy cavalry tactics were decisive against Irish infantry and chariot warfare; the combination of motte-and-bailey castles and mounted knights allowed rapid pacification of the lowlands

Grants of Irish land to Anglo-Norman magnates (de Lacy, Marshal, de Burgh) created a feudal network in eastern Ireland; Dublin as an administrative center and the Pale as a defended English zone maintained an effective, if limited, English presence

Richard de Clare (Strongbow)'s invasion (1169–70), invited by Diarmait Mac Murchada, established Norman control of Leinster. Henry II's subsequent arrival (1171) turned a private Norman conquest into an English royal lordship, though direct control remained limited.

Ireland exported wool, hides, and cattle to English and continental markets. The Pale (English-controlled eastern zone) developed as an agricultural surplus area feeding English urban markets, providing economic rationale for continued English presence.

Pope Adrian IV's bull Laudabiliter (1155) granted Henry II of England lordship over Ireland; his actual expedition in 1171–72 established the basis for English governance with Irish kings rendering formal submission.

The English colonial network established new walled boroughs, Kilkenny, Cork, Waterford, Drogheda, that channeled Irish agricultural exports through English-controlled ports generating customs revenues that funded the Lordship's administration.

decline_factors.description: Anglo-Norman lords in Ireland rapidly became independent of English royal control, adopting Irish customs, law, and alliances; the 'degenerate English' who 'went native' undermined the project of English governance from within

The Black Death hit English settlements hardest; Gaelic lords recovered land and independence in the 14th century; by 1400 English control was limited to the Pale around Dublin; the Statutes of Kilkenny (1366) acknowledged the failure of cultural assimilation

English lords with Irish holdings prioritized English politics and estates; lords-lieutenant changed frequently; the lack of sustained royal attention allowed Anglo-Norman families (the Old English) to become semi-autonomous Gaelic lords themselves

The area of effective English control contracted throughout the 14th–15th centuries to a shrinking "Pale" around Dublin, with the Statutes of Kilkenny (1366) demonstrating how thoroughly Gaelic culture had re-established itself beyond English jurisdiction.

description: Principality of Hungary (895–1000), nomadic Magyar confederation that settled the Carpathian Basin after migrating from the Pontic steppe; the Battle of Lechfeld (955) ended Magyar raids into western Europe and opened the path to Christianisation under Géza and Stephen I, whose 1000 CE papal coronation transformed the confederation into a Christian feudal kingdom integrated into European diplomatic networks.

temporal.notes: Stub: dates from GeoJSON basemap years 700–1000

lifecycle_phases.description: Ugrian-speaking Magyar tribes migrated westward from the Ural region; settled in the Pontic steppe before the Pecheneg invasion.
Magyar tribes crossed the Carpathians into the Pannonian plain (895) after Pechenegs destroyed their steppe homeland.
Magyar cavalry raided throughout western Europe, reaching Spain and southern Italy; finally stopped at the Battle of Lechfeld (955).
Christianisation under Géza and Stephen I; Hungary established as a Christian kingdom (1000).

rise_factors.description: Magyar horse archers were among the most mobile warriors in Europe; effective across vast raid distances.
The Carpathian Basin provided a defensible base with rich agricultural potential after settlement.

decline_factors.description: Otto I's victory at Lechfeld (955) ended the raiding era and forced Magyar political transformation.
Conversion to Christianity ended the mobile raiding economy and required integration into feudal European norms.

description: Nubian Christian kingdom of Makuria (c. 4th–14th c.) centred on Old Dongola that successfully resisted Arab expansion through the Baqt treaty (652), which kept Egypt's Muslim rulers from conquering Nubia for six centuries; Makuria's Coptic-influenced monastic church-building programme and diplomatic skill in mediating between Egypt and sub-Saharan Africa maintained Christian culture in the Nile valley long after Egypt's Islamisation.

lifecycle_phases.description: Makuria emerged as a Nubian Christian kingdom on the middle Nile; formed from the ancient Meroitic tradition.
Makurian King Mercurios defeated an Arab invasion and signed the Baqt treaty with Egypt (651); flourished as a Christian buffer state.
Gradual Arabisation and Islamisation of northern Sudan; Mamluk Egypt intervened increasingly in Makurian succession.
Last Christian Makurian king replaced by a Muslim ruler under Mamluk pressure; kingdom dissolved.

rise_factors.description: The Baqt agreement with Arab Egypt provided stable borders and trade for three centuries.
Coptic Christianity connected Makuria to Egypt's intellectual and material resources.

decline_factors.description: Arab migration into northern Sudan and conversion of nobility eroded the Christian ruling class.
Mamluks installed Muslim kings and progressively subordinated Makuria to Egyptian interests.

description: West African empire (c. 1235–1600) founded by Sundiata Keita after the Battle of Kirina; controlling the gold and salt trade across the Sahara, Mali's rulers including Mansa Musa (famous 1324 pilgrimage) accumulated legendary wealth, sponsored Islamic scholarship at Timbuktu and Djenné, and governed a multi-ethnic empire stretching from the Atlantic to the Niger Bend through a sophisticated provincial administration.

lifecycle_phases.description: Sundiata Keita defeats Ghana at Kirina; consolidates Manding chieftaincies into centralised empire controlling upper Niger
Mansa Musa's reign (1312–1337), pilgrimage to Mecca publicises Malian wealth; Timbuktu and Djenné become Islamic scholarly centres; territorial maximum
Succession conflicts weaken central authority; Tuareg raids from north; Mossi raids from south erode borderlands
Songhay (Songhai) Empire absorbs Timbuktu and the Niger Bend; Mali retreats to its Manding heartland around Niani

rise_factors.description: Mali controlled the trans-Saharan gold-salt exchange at its source, monopolising gold from Bambuk and Bure mines
Malian emperors' adoption of Islam integrated them into the Islamic scholarly network and legitimised governance for Muslim merchant communities
Sundiata's cavalry and infantry alliance system unified the Manding clans into a professional military force unlike earlier Ghana's informal levies

decline_factors.description: Post-Musa succession conflicts produced multiple simultaneous claimants who hired Tuareg mercenaries, draining treasury and enabling raids
Songhay Sunni Ali's conquests absorbed the Niger Bend trade cities that were Mali's primary revenue source

description: Military slave dynasty ruling Egypt and Syria (1250–1517) that halted the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut (1260), the first significant defeat of a Mongol army in the field, and systematically dismantled the remaining Crusader states; its devşirme-like system of slave soldiers who rose to command created a meritocratic military elite that provided Egypt with its most stable medieval governance.

temporal.notes: Mamluk slave-soldiers overthrow last Ayyubid sultan 1250; defeat Mongols at Ain Jalut 1260; expel last Crusaders 1291; conquered by Ottoman Sultan Selim I 1517

lifecycle_phases.description: Baybars (r.1260–1277) halts the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut (1260); systematically destroys Crusader castles and ports; installs a shadow Abbasid caliph in Cairo for religious legitimacy; creates an efficient postal relay (barid) system across Egypt and Syria

Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad (r.1310–1341) presides over a cultural and commercial golden age; Cairo becomes the largest city west of China; the Red Sea spice trade dominates Mamluk revenues; fall of Acre (1291) completes the destruction of the Crusader states

Circassian Burji dynasty replaces Bahri Mamluks; Black Death devastation of 1340s permanently weakens the economy; Portuguese circumnavigation of Africa (1497) diverts spice trade; Ottoman firearms technology defeats Mamluk cavalry at Marj Dabiq (1516) and Ridaniyya (1517)

rise_factors.description: Mamluk cavalry (trained slave-soldiers from childhood) were among the finest heavy cavalry in the medieval world; victory at Ain Jalut (1260) was the first major Mongol defeat, demonstrating their tactical superiority

Controlled the Red Sea–Indian Ocean spice trade routes; Cairo under al-Nasir Muhammad was the wealthiest city in the world, with revenues from silk, spices, and grain funding a vast military-bureaucratic apparatus
Hosted the shadow Abbasid caliphate in Cairo after 1261; position as guardians of the Holy Cities (Mecca and Medina) and the most powerful Sunni state gave immense religious prestige

The Mamluk defeat of the Mongol army at Ain Jalut in 1260, the first major Mongol defeat in open battle, halted Mongol expansion into Africa and established Mamluk military dominance in the eastern Mediterranean.

The Mamluk system of purchasing and training enslaved Turkish and Circassian soldiers created a professional military caste with intense esprit de corps, technically superior horsemanship, and political cohesion unmatched by feudal European armies.

decline_factors.description: The Black Death (1347–1349) killed approximately one-third of Egypt's population; repeated plague recurrences throughout the 14th and 15th centuries permanently reduced agricultural output and military manpower

Mamluk cavalry culture rejected firearms as dishonorable; the Ottomans' systematic use of artillery and muskets at Marj Dabiq (1516) and Ridaniyya (1517) made the Mamluk cavalry charge tactically obsolete
Portuguese discovery of the Cape of Good Hope route to India (1497–1498) gradually diverted the spice trade away from Egyptian ports, fatally undermining the fiscal basis of Mamluk power

Vasco da Gama's rounding of the Cape of Good Hope (1498) bypassed the Mamluk-controlled Levantine trade routes, diverting spice revenues to Portugal and collapsing the commercial basis of Mamluk power.
The Mamluks refused to adopt field artillery as beneath warrior dignity; Ottoman cannon devastated their cavalry at Marj Dābiq (1516) and Ridaniyya (1517), completing the conquest in two campaigns.

description: North German frontier march (1157–1618) created by Albert the Bear's conquest of Slavic territories; its position at the Elbe-Oder crossing made it the springboard for German eastward colonisation, while the Hohenzollern acquisition (1415) began the dynasty that would eventually create modern Germany, making Brandenburg a pivotal hinge in European history.

temporal.notes: Type mapped to principality (margraviate not in schema enum).

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Albert the Bear conquers Brandenburg from the Slavic Hevelli.
Ascanian expansion east and north; Brandenburg a major imperial electorate.
Dynastic transfers: Wittelsbach, Luxembourg; sold to Hohenzollern 1415.

rise_factors.description: German Ostsiedlung eastward colonization provided settlers, capital, and economic development of new territories.
Albert the Bear established the Ascanian military march with systematic castle-building and garrison organization.
Ascanian margraves systematically acquired adjacent Slavic territories through warfare and purchase.
The Hohenzollern dynasty acquired Brandenburg in 1415 and systematically built up centralized administration, integrating the scattered Ascanian inheritance into a coherent territorial state.

Brandenburg's position on the North German Plain gave it control over river crossings and roads linking the Rhine, Oder, and Vistula river systems, strategic importance that justified sustained imperial investment in its defense.

decline_factors.description: Ascanian line died out in 1320, leaving Brandenburg contested between Wittelsbach and Luxembourg dynasties.
Brandenburg was divided and sold among competing dynastic claims through the 14th century.
Repeated changes of ruling house undermined institutional continuity.

Brandenburg suffered extreme devastation during the Thirty Years War (1618–48), with half its population dying from war, plague, and famine, temporarily making it one of the most depopulated regions in Central Europe.

The margraviate was superseded by the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701 when Elector Frederick III crowned himself King in Prussia, elevating Brandenburg from a march to the nucleus of a major European power.

description: Berber Marinid sultanate of Morocco (1244–1465) that succeeded the Almohads; controlled Morocco and periodically intervened in Iberia to support the Granada emirate against Castile; major patrons of Islamic architecture including the Bou Inania madrasas; weakened by internal succession conflicts and Iberian pressure.

lifecycle_phases.description: Marinids defeat the Almohads and seize Marrakesh (1269), establishing control over Morocco; tribal Zenata Berber warriors form the military core

Abu Yusuf Ya'qub captures Fez (1248) and builds New Fez; repeatedly intervenes in al-Andalus to defend Granada; defeated at Rio Salado (1340) by combined Castilian-Portuguese forces; massive building program of madrasas, mosques, and city walls
Fragmentation into rival Marinid branches; Wattasid viziers gain effective power; final Marinid sultan overthrown 1465

rise_factors.description: The Almohad Caliphate's military defeats in Iberia and internal religious schisms left Morocco ungoverned; the Marinids filled the vacuum with disciplined Zenata Berber cavalry
Morocco's position at the northern terminus of trans-Saharan gold and slave routes gave the Marinids revenues that funded their building program and military campaigns
Marinid sultans built madrasas at Fez, Salé, and Meknes, positioning themselves as champions of Sunni Maliki scholarship and attracting scholars from across the Islamic world including Ibn Khaldun

decline_factors.description: The crushing defeat at Rio Salado (1340) ended Marinid ambitions in Iberia and undermined the sultans' prestige as defenders of Islam against the Reconquista
Repeated succession conflicts between Marinid princes depopulated cities, emptied treasuries, and allowed Wattasid viziers to dominate the sultanate
The plague struck Morocco in the 1340s, described vividly by Ibn Khaldun; it killed large portions of the urban and military population on which Marinid power rested

description: Mayapan was the last major Maya pre-Hispanic capital, founded after the abandonment of Chichen Itza and dominating northern Yucatán from c. 1221 until c. 1441. Unlike its Classic-period predecessors, the city was a tightly walled compact settlement of ~12,000 inhabitants, with elite residential compounds clustered around a smaller-scale temple core that copied Chichen Itza's monuments. Mayapan operated as the seat of a loose 'league' of provincial Maya rulers (the multepal system) until factional war between the Cocom and Xiu dynasties destroyed it; the surviving Maya kingdoms of Yucatán fragmented into the ~16 cuchcabaloob the Spanish encountered.

temporal.notes: Conventional dating: Mayapan founded c. 1221 after the abandonment of Chichen Itza, abandoned itself after the Cocom-Xiu war c. 1441.

lifecycle_phases.description: Mayapan founded as new northern Yucatán capital after Chichen Itza's abandonment.
Peak, Cocom dynasty dominates the multepal council of provincial lords.
Xiu revolt against Cocom dominance; city sacked and abandoned c. 1441.

rise_factors.description: The multepal council of provincial lords centralised in Mayapan gave northern Yucatán a single political node for ~two centuries.
Mayapan's elites consciously echoed Chichen Itza's monumental forms to claim continuity with the prior northern Maya hegemony.

decline_factors.description: The Xiu revolt against Cocom rule c. 1441 destroyed Mayapan and fragmented northern Yucatán into the cuchcabaloob.

secondary_bases: salt extraction from northern Yucatán coast

description: Network of independent and shifting city-states across the southern Maya lowlands and adjacent highlands, sharing a writing system, ritual calendar, and material culture. Major centres, Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán, Caracol, competed and allied through dynastic marriages and protracted wars. The Late Classic period saw extensive monumental construction; the ninth-century collapse depopulated most of the southern lowland centres while the northern Yucatán transitioned into the Postclassic.

temporal.notes: Classic Maya civilisation spans roughly 250–900 CE; within the atlas scope (500–1500) from 500 to the Classic collapse ~900. Succeeded by the Postclassic Maya polities.

geographic.notes: Centroid set near Tikal in the Petén lowlands; territory was a constellation of city-states (Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán, Caracol) rather than a single contiguous realm.

description: Successor polities to the Classic Maya collapse, centred on the northern Yucatán (Chichén Itzá, Mayapán, Uxmal) and the Guatemalan highlands (K'iche', Kaqchikel). The Postclassic was politically more fragmented than the Classic but maintained extensive long-distance trade networks reaching central Mexico and lower Central America. Mayapán's fall around 1441 left a constellation of small contending kingdoms encountered by Spanish expeditions after 1517.

temporal.notes: Postclassic Maya polities succeeded the Classic collapse in the northern Yucatán and Guatemalan highlands; ran to Spanish contact (1517 onward, beyond atlas scope).

geographic.notes: Centroid near Chichén Itzá; later capitals included Mayapán (~1220–1440) and the K'iche' centre Q'umarkaj in the highlands.

description: First Frankish dynasty (481–751) founded by Clovis I whose conversion to Nicene Christianity (496) aligned the Franks with Rome against Arian Germanic rivals; through centuries of fragmentation, civil war, and gradual power loss to the Carolingian mayors of the palace, the Merovingians nonetheless transmitted Roman administrative traditions into post-Roman governance and established the Frankish kingdom as the dominant power in western Europe.

temporal.notes: Frankish kingdom under the Merovingian dynasty

lifecycle_phases.description: Clovis I defeats the last Roman governor (486), Visigoths at Vouillé (507), and converts to Catholic Christianity, the first Germanic king to do so. His baptism gives the Franks papal support over Arian rivals. Frankish kingdom expands across modern France and western Germany.

After Dagobert I's death (639), Merovingian kings become figureheads ('do-nothing kings') while the Carolingian family, as Mayors of the Palace, hold real power. Charles Martel defeats the Umayyads at Tours (732) without being king. His son Pippin III deposes the last Merovingian with papal blessing (751).

rise_factors.description: Clovis I's conversion to Catholic Christianity (498) was the decisive differentiator from Arian Visigoth and Ostrogoth rivals; papal support gave Frankish expansion in Gaul divine sanction over other Germanic kingdoms

Frankish mixed tactics (heavy infantry with francisca throwing axes, backed by cavalry) proved superior to both Roman remnant forces and other Germanic armies; victory at Vouillé (507) destroyed Visigothic power in France

Clovis I's defeat of Syagrius (486), the Visigoths (507), and the Alamanni unified northern Gaul under Frankish rule within a generation, establishing territorial dominance over the most productive region of post-Roman Europe.

Clovis's Catholic baptism (c.496), unlike Arian Visigoths and Ostrogoths, made him the champion of Nicene Christianity among Gallo-Roman bishops and clergy, who cooperated enthusiastically in Frankish administration.

Clovis I's conversion to Catholic Christianity around 496 gave him the support of the Gallo-Roman bishops who controlled literacy, administration, and the loyalty of the romanized population, the institutional foundation for Frankish governance.

decline_factors.description: Frankish inheritance custom divided the kingdom among all sons, producing endemic civil war between sub-kingdoms (Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy); repeated partitions made Merovingian kings dependent on aristocratic support
Power transferred to hereditary Mayors of the Palace; the Carolingian family's military effectiveness under Charles Martel and Pippin III made the nominal kingship vestigial

From the 7th century, Merovingian kings ("rois fainéants") became ceremonial figureheads while Carolingian mayors of the palace exercised real power. The dynasty lost the ability to enforce succession decisions or raise armies independently.

Frankish inheritance custom divided kingdoms among all royal sons. Multiple Merovingian partitions (511, 561, 613, 714) produced chronic civil wars between sub-kingdoms, depleting the dynasty's military capacity and political cohesion.

The later Merovingian kings (rois fainéants) were politically marginalized by the Carolingian mayors of the palace, who concentrated actual power in their own hands; Pepin the Short's deposition of the last Merovingian in 751 formalized a transfer that had been complete for decades.

population_estimates.note: Triple Alliance tributary population at peak; Tenochtitlan resident population ~200,000.

description: Triple Alliance of the Mexica (Tenochtitlan), Acolhua (Texcoco), and Tepanec (Tlacopan), ascendant in the Valley of Mexico after the 1428 victory over Azcapotzalco and expanded under successive tlatoani, Itzcoatl, Moctezuma I, Axayacatl, Tizoc, Ahuitzotl, Moctezuma II, to a tributary hegemony across much of central and southern Mexico. The empire collected tribute through a network of conquered city-states rather than direct administration, and ran on a calendar of recurrent military campaigns tied to ritual sacrifice.

temporal.notes: Founding of Tenochtitlan traditionally dated 1325; the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan formed in 1428. The polity fell to the Spanish-Tlaxcalan siege in 1521; within atlas scope to 1500.

geographic.notes: Capital Tenochtitlan on the island in Lake Texcoco, the site of modern Mexico City.

lifecycle_phases.description: Mexica found Tenochtitlan on Lake Texcoco; vassals of Azcapotzalco until 1428.
Itzcoatl and Tlacaelel forge the Triple Alliance after the defeat of Azcapotzalco.
Moctezuma I extends tribute reach into Veracruz and the Mixteca; Flower Wars institutionalised.
Axayacatl, Tizoc, and Ahuitzotl extend reach to the Pacific and into Oaxaca; Templo Mayor rebuilt.
Moctezuma II accedes (1502); centralising reforms tighten Mexica primacy over the other two capitals. Spanish-Tlaxcalan siege ends the polity in 1521.

rise_factors.description: Cuachic warrior orders and tributary-province military service produced a standing army deployable in mass campaigns.
Standardised tribute lists from ~38 provinces underwrote monumental construction and elite consumption.
State theology centred on Huitzilopochtli and the cosmic necessity of human sacrifice tied military victory to the survival of the world.

decline_factors.description: Cortés's 1519 expedition + Tlaxcalan alliance + smallpox introduced 1520 culminated in the siege of Tenochtitlan and the polity's destruction.

sources.author: Smith, Michael E.
sources.title: The Aztecs

description: Short-lived Carolingian middle kingdom (843–855) created by the Treaty of Verdun for Lothar I, comprising Italy, Burgundy, Provence, and the Rhine corridor; its rapid fragmentation among Lothar's sons and eventual absorption by East and West Francia proved the impossibility of maintaining a viable middle kingdom between the two dominant Carolingian successors.

temporal.notes: Short-lived; partitioned at Treaty of Meerssen 870

lifecycle_phases.description: The Treaty of Verdun (843) divides the Carolingian Empire among Louis the Pious's three surviving sons: Louis the German gets East Francia, Charles the Bald gets West Francia, and Lothair I gets the middle strip, 'Middle Francia' or Lotharingia, including Italy, Burgundy, Provence, and the Rhine corridor. It is an artificial creation designed to give the eldest (Lothair) the dignity of emperor and Rome. Lothair's son Lothair II rules Lorraine (Lotharingia); his death without legitimate heirs (869) leads to the Treaty of Meerssen (870), dividing Middle Francia between East and West Francia.

Lothair I retains the imperial title alongside Middle Francia, but the title provides symbolic weight without coherent governance. His court at Aachen attempts to maintain Carolingian administrative traditions, but the empire lacks the geographic compactness needed for effective rule across its Italian, Burgundian, and Lotharingian territories.

rise_factors.description: Middle Francia existed solely as a diplomatic compromise at the Treaty of Verdun (843); Lothair I received it as the portion due the eldest son and Holy Roman Emperor, not because of any organic political unity in the territory

Middle Francia was created by the Treaty of Verdun (843) as a compromise to prevent civil war between Louis the Pious's sons; Lothar I received it as the eldest son's share, including the imperial title and the two traditional Carolingian heartlands (Aachen and Rome)

The Rhine and Rhône valleys formed the commercial spine of Middle Francia; control of these river arteries meant control of the most important trade routes between the North Sea and the Mediterranean, giving whoever held them structural economic advantages

As the heir to Charlemagne's imperial title, Middle Francia's rulers possessed the most powerful legitimizing claim in Christendom; the imperial title attracted the allegiance of German bishops, Italian magnates, and border lords who wanted connection to imperial dignity

The Treaty of Verdun (843) created Middle Francia for Lothair I as the eldest Carolingian brother, giving him an elongated realm stretching from the North Sea to central Italy including the imperial capital Aachen and Rome.

decline_factors.description: Lothair II's death without legitimate heirs (869) was the fundamental cause of Middle Francia's dissolution; the Treaty of Meerssen (870) divided the territory between East and West Francia because there was no legitimate heir to inherit it as a unit

Middle Francia was never a coherent political unit; it stretched from the Low Countries to Rome, containing distinct regions (Lorraine, Burgundy, Provence, Italy) with no shared language, culture, or administrative tradition

Lothar I partitioned Middle Francia among his three sons in 855, Louis got Italy, Charles got Provence/Burgundy, Lothar II got Lorraine; this three-way split destroyed the political coherence that had barely held the middle kingdom together and invited East and West Frankish predation

Middle Francia had no natural geographic unity; stretching from Frisia to the Po valley, it lacked the Rhine frontier of East Francia or the Seine basin of West Francia; without a defensible core, it was a collection of territories whose neighbors systematically absorbed them

On Lothair I's death in 855 Middle Francia was divided among his three sons: Louis II received Italy, Charles Provence, and Lothair II got Lotharingia, dismembering the central kingdom that had theoretically balanced east and west.

population_estimates.note: Hongwu-era census figures are widely held to undercount; estimates range from 60 to 75 million.
Mid-Ming demographic peak before the late-Ming late-16th century surge.

description: Han Chinese dynasty (1368–1644) founded when Zhu Yuanzhang (Hongwu Emperor) drove the Yuan Mongols out of Khanbaliq and reclaimed the imperial throne for an ethnically Chinese ruling house; the early Ming consolidated under Hongwu's reorganisation of the bureaucracy and the Yongle Emperor's relocation of the capital to Beijing, his construction of the Forbidden City, his rebuilding of the Great Wall in its modern stone form, and his sponsorship of Zheng He's seven maritime expeditions (1405–1433); within the atlas's 1500 horizon the dynasty is at its mid-period institutional peak, with the civil-service examination system, Neo-Confucian orthodoxy, porcelain export industry, and a population approaching 110 million all defining a recognisably early-modern Chinese state.

temporal.notes: Founded by Zhu Yuanzhang (Hongwu Emperor) after overthrowing the Yuan; ruled China to 1644, beyond the atlas's 1500 horizon.

lifecycle_phases.description: Hongwu Emperor expels the Yuan from Khanbaliq, restores Han rule, rebuilds the civil service examination system, reorganises the army into hereditary military households (weisuo).

Yongle Emperor moves the capital from Nanjing to Beijing, builds the Forbidden City, restores the Grand Canal, commissions Zheng He's treasure voyages to the Indian Ocean, and rebuilds the Great Wall in stone.
Post-Yongle retrenchment: maritime expeditions cancelled (1433), inward-looking Confucian bureaucracy stabilises into a long mid-period; population and economy continue to grow.

description: Network of Mixtec-speaking city-states and small kingdoms (señoríos) across the Mixteca region of present-day Oaxaca, ascendant after the contraction of Monte Albán and famous for codex-based historical record-keeping, fine metalwork, and the legendary career of the eleventh-century warlord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw. Several Mixtec polities fell tributary to the Mexica in the late fifteenth century without losing internal political organisation.

temporal.notes: Postclassic Mixtec city-states and small kingdoms across the Mixteca region; some annexed by the Mexica in the late fifteenth century but retained local political identity to Spanish contact.

geographic.notes: Centroid set in the Mixteca Alta highlands; political authority was distributed across many small señoríos rather than concentrated at a single capital.

description: Largest contiguous land empire in history (1206–1368) founded by Genghis Khan; its military innovations, combined arms tactics, siege engineering, psychological warfare, conquered territory from Korea to Poland; while destructive, its Pax Mongolica created the conditions for the first sustained Eurasian trade network, and its successor states shaped Persian, Chinese, Russian, and Turkish civilisations profoundly.

temporal.notes: Founded by Genghis Khan 1206; fragmented into four khanates; Yuan dynasty falls 1368

lifecycle_phases.description: Genghis Khan unites Mongol tribes; conquers northern China, Khwarezmian Empire, and Kievan Rus
Sons and grandsons complete conquest of China, Persia, Baghdad (1258), and invade Poland and Hungary
Empire splits into four khanates: Golden Horde, Ilkhanate, Chagatai Khanate, Yuan Dynasty; lose cohesion

rise_factors.description: Mongol cavalry combined extreme mobility with coordinated tactics, devastating settled armies across Eurasia
Decimal organization (arbans, jaghuns, mingghans, tumens), meritocratic promotion, and sophisticated siege warfare technology
Exploited political fragmentation of Jin China, Kievan Rus, and Islamic world to divide and conquer

Genghis Khan reorganized the Mongol army on decimal units (arban 10, zuun 100, myangan 1000, tumen 10,000) cutting across tribal lines. This disrupted inter-tribal conflict and created a professional military hierarchy loyal to the Khan rather than tribal chiefs.

The Yasa (Great Law) codified Mongol customary law, creating uniform legal standards across conquered territories. Its pragmatic tolerance, protecting merchants, exempting clergy, guaranteeing messenger safety, made Mongol governance predictable and commerce-friendly.

At its height, the Mongol Empire created the largest free trade zone in history: the Pax Mongolica (c.1250–1350) allowed merchants to travel from China to Europe under Mongol protection, carrying silk, spices, and plague-carrying rats.

Mongol commanders systematically used terror as strategic policy: cities that surrendered received lenient treatment; those that resisted were massacred to the last inhabitant. This made subsequent cities far more likely to surrender, dramatically reducing siege costs.

decline_factors.description: No clear succession mechanism; civil wars between Genghis Khan's descendants led to permanent fragmentation
Vast overextension across Eurasia made integrated governance impossible; regional khanates became independent

Mongol succession required a kurultai (assembly of princes) to elect the next Khan. This consensus requirement became unworkable as the empire grew: regional khans refused to attend, recognized different successors, and succession wars became endemic after Möngke Khan's death (1259).

The Black Death originated in Mongol-controlled Central Asia (c.1346) and spread along Mongol-maintained trade routes. The devastation reduced Mongol population across Eurasia and disrupted the administrative networks that held the empire together.

population_estimates.note: Japanese demography is poorly documented in this period; estimates vary widely.
Pre-Sengoku-collapse aggregate; Ōnin War destruction concentrated in the capital region.

description: Second Japanese shogunate (1336–1573), founded by Ashikaga Takauji after he turned against Emperor Go-Daigo's Kenmu Restoration and established a rival imperial line in Kyoto; the early Ashikaga period was defined by the Nanboku-chō split (1336–1392) between the Northern Court at Kyoto and the Southern Court at Yoshino, resolved when the third shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu negotiated the reunification of the imperial lines and built the Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion); the mid-15th century saw a high cultural flowering, Zen monastery influence, the Higashiyama culture of the eighth shogun Yoshimasa, the Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion), tea ceremony and noh theatre take shape, followed by the catastrophic Ōnin War (1467–1477) that destroyed Kyoto and inaugurated the Sengoku (Warring States) period during which the bakufu's central authority collapsed even as Ashikaga shoguns continued to nominally hold the title; within the atlas's 1500 horizon the shogunate is mid-Sengoku, in name only.

temporal.notes: Founded by Ashikaga Takauji after the Kenmu Restoration; named for the Muromachi district of Kyoto where the third shogun moved the bakufu palace; ruled to 1573, beyond the atlas's 1500 horizon.

lifecycle_phases.description: Ashikaga Takauji breaks with Emperor Go-Daigo, establishes a rival emperor in Kyoto (Northern Court); the Southern Court at Yoshino contests legitimacy until reunification under Yoshimitsu in 1392.
Ashikaga Yoshimitsu unifies the imperial courts (1392), accepts the title 'King of Japan' from Ming China, builds Kinkaku-ji; Zen Buddhism and tea culture flourish.
Higashiyama culture under Yoshimasa; Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion) built; shugo daimyō become more autonomous in the provinces; central bakufu finance and authority erode.

Ōnin War (1467–1477) destroys Kyoto and triggers the Sengoku period; central authority disintegrates while shoguns remain nominally in office; the bakufu's actual power survives only in the Kinai region around the capital.

description: Historic port of Oman (various polities, settled antiquity onward) that served as the main entrepôt for the Arabian Sea trade between India, East Africa, and the Persian Gulf; its strategic position at the mouth of the Gulf made it contested between Portuguese, Omani Yarubid, Safavid Persian, and later Omani Bu Saidi imams; the Ibadi Imamate tradition that characterises Oman's political culture has roots in the early Islamic period.

lifecycle_phases.description: Ibadi Islamic state formed in Oman; Muscat was a key port for Indian Ocean trade.
Muscat and Sohar were major entrepots linking Persian Gulf trade to the Indian Ocean network.
Rise of the Kingdom of Hormuz as a rival Gulf commercial power reduced Muscat's relative importance.

rise_factors.description: Muscat's sheltered harbour was one of the finest on the Arabian Sea coast.
Ibadi Islam created a distinct mercantile identity linked to diaspora communities across the Indian Ocean.

decline_factors.description: Hormuz emerged as the dominant Gulf entrepot, diverting trade away from Muscat.

description: Kingdom of Nanzhao (738–902) in present-day Yunnan, founded by Piluoge who unified six southern Zhao kingdoms; positioned between Tang China and Tibet, Nanzhao alternately allied with each while maintaining independence, defeating Tang armies at the Battle of Tali (754) and absorbing Buddhist and Tang cultural influences; it was replaced by the Kingdom of Dali which maintained similar independence until Mongol conquest (1253).

lifecycle_phases.description: Piluoge unifies six southern Zhao kingdoms with Tang support; Nanzhao kingdom established at Taihe
Defeats Tang punitive expeditions (754, 763); independent diplomacy between Tang and Tibet; Buddhist culture from both directions adopted
Dali succeeding kingdom weakens before absorption; Tang collapse removes the enemy that gave Nanzhao geopolitical relevance
Nanzhao replaced by Great Changhe then Dali Kingdom, which continues its cultural tradition until Mongol conquest in 1253

rise_factors.description: Yunnan plateau position between Tang China and Tibet allowed Nanzhao to play both powers against each other while controlling the Yunnan trade route to Southeast Asia

decline_factors.description: Internal coup replaced founding Mengshe dynasty with the Zheng family, weakening legitimacy and ultimately dissolving Nanzhao into its Dali successor state

description: Viking Norse settlements on Greenland's western coast (c. 985–c. 1408) established by Erik the Red; their survival for four centuries depended on a fragile pastoral economy supplemented by Arctic trade goods, walrus ivory, furs, live polar bears, that eventually became economically marginal as African ivory recovered, leaving the settlements isolated until their mysterious disappearance in the fifteenth century.

temporal.notes: Eastern and Western Settlements; gradual decline and disappearance

geographic.no_central_capital_reason: Dispersed Norse farms at Brattahlíð and Garðar; no centralised seat.

lifecycle_phases.description: Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, establishes two Norse settlements on Greenland's southwest coast (985): the Eastern Settlement (Eystribyggð) near modern Narsarsuaq and the Western Settlement (Vestribyggð) near modern Nuuk. At peak, 3,000–5,000 Norse settlers raise cattle, hunt walrus, and export furs and ivory to Norway. The Eastern Settlement's church at Garðar has a cathedral; Greenland becomes a bishopric (1124).

The Little Ice Age (c.1300) makes Greenland progressively colder; sea ice blocks the shipping lanes. The Black Death (1349–1350) in Norway disrupts the supply ships that Greenland depended on. The Western Settlement is abandoned by c.1350. Inuit (Thule culture) migration southward brings a technologically superior cold-weather culture into contact with the Norse. The Eastern Settlement disappears; the last dated written record from Norse Greenland is 1408.

rise_factors.description: Greenlandic walrus ivory was the finest ivory available in medieval Europe, elephant ivory being rare and expensive; Greenlandic hunting parties in the High Arctic brought back walrus tusks, polar bear skins, and white falcons that commanded premium prices in European markets

Erik the Red's deliberate colonization of Greenland (c. 985) established two settlement clusters, the Eastern and Western Settlements, organized around pastoral farming; the settlements' survival for over four centuries in marginal conditions demonstrates the Norse capacity for adaptive colonization

Greenlandic walrus ivory was among the most prized luxury materials in medieval Europe; it funded church construction (the cathedral at Gardar), episcopal appointments, and royal Norwegian tribute through a trade that connected the Arctic to the Mediterranean market

Greenland received its own bishop (Diocese of Gardar, established c. 1124) and eventually had 12 parish churches; church buildings of dressed stone represented an extraordinary capital investment for the small population and anchored Norse identity and organization

Norse Greenland supplied Europe with walrus ivory, narwhal tusks, polar bear skins, and live falcons, luxury goods commanding extraordinary prices that made even a small community commercially viable.

decline_factors.description: The Medieval Warm Period (c.900–1300) that made Greenland settlement viable gave way to the Little Ice Age; advancing sea ice blocked shipping lanes and the growing season shortened, making Norse cattle farming marginal while the Inuit's seal-hunting culture proved more adaptable

African elephant ivory flowing through Italian merchant networks gradually replaced Greenlandic walrus ivory in European markets; the Black Death's disruption of Norwegian shipping networks severed Greenland's commercial lifeline at the worst possible moment

Cooling temperatures from the 13th century reduced the growing season and increased sea ice; the Norse farming system, adapted to Scandinavian conditions, could not adjust quickly enough, and reduced haymaking meant the cattle herds could not survive increasingly harsh winters

The reopening of African elephant ivory trade in the 13th century collapsed the price of walrus ivory; Greenland's sole export commodity was devalued just as the colony needed resources to cope with climate deterioration, removing the economic rationale for maintaining the settlement

The reopening of African elephant ivory trade routes in the 14th century crashed walrus ivory prices, eliminating Greenland's primary commercial advantage precisely as the climate cooled and sailing conditions worsened.

sources.author: Reuter, Timothy (ed.)
sources.title: The New Cambridge Medieval History, Vol. III: c. 900 – c. 1024

description: Personal union of England, Denmark, and Norway under Cnut the Great (1016–1035) representing the apex of Viking political achievement; Cnut's transformation from conquering warlord to Christian king, pilgrimage to Rome, church patronage, law code, demonstrated Scandinavian political sophistication, but the empire dissolved immediately after his death from inheritance division.

temporal.notes: Cnut the Great's personal union; dissolved at his death

lifecycle_phases.description: Cnut the Great, son of Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark, completes the Danish conquest of England (1016) after years of campaigning by his father. He defeats Edmund Ironside and becomes King of England. Inheriting Denmark (1018), he adds Norway (1028) and claims suzerainty over part of Scotland. The North Sea Empire, England, Denmark, Norway, and part of Sweden, is the greatest Scandinavian achievement.

Cnut's death (1035) produces immediate succession conflict among his sons. Harold I Harefoot rules England (1035–1040) against opposition from Harthacanut in Denmark. Harthacanut's accession (1040) and sudden death without heirs (1042) ends the Danish line; Edward the Confessor (from the Anglo-Saxon Wessex line) is invited back as king, ending the North Sea Empire after only 26 years.

rise_factors.description: Cnut's military victories, against the English fyrd at Assandun (1016) and later campaigns, demonstrated the superiority of Scandinavian naval mobility combined with English land forces; his huscarls (professional household troops) were the best infantry in northern Europe

Cnut governed England through Anglo-Saxon institutions rather than replacing them, issuing laws in the tradition of Edgar the Peaceful and patronizing the English Church, which gave his rule domestic legitimacy that pure conquest would not have provided

Canute's conquest of England (1016) and Denmark (1018–1019) was accomplished through a combination of decisive battlefield victory (Assandun, 1016), strategic marriage (Emma of Normandy), and shrewd incorporation of existing English administrative structures; he ruled as an English king with English traditions

The North Sea Empire united the two shores of England's primary trade corridor; English wool and silver, Danish amber and furs, Norwegian timber and dried fish all moved within the same political sphere, reducing the transaction costs and piracy risks that had impeded trade

England's Church was the wealthiest in northern Europe and a sophisticated administrative institution; Canute's patronage of English monasteries and support for the English Church bought ecclesiastical loyalty and gave him administrative tools (literate clerks, estate management) unavailable in Scandinavia

Cnut the Great's conquest of England (1016) unified Denmark, England, and Norway in a single North Sea commercial and political empire that controlled the richest herring fisheries, the most productive silver mines, and the most advanced urban economies of northern Europe.

decline_factors.description: Cnut's empire depended entirely on his personal rule; his three sons Harold Harefoot, Harthacanut, and Sweyn immediately competed for the inheritance, and Harthacanut's death without heirs in 1042 ended the dynasty entirely

Canute's early death (1035) left his empire to quarreling sons, Harold Harefoot took England, Harthacnut Denmark; within seven years both were dead, and Edward the Confessor (Anglo-Saxon Wessex) reclaimed England; the empire required Canute's personal genius and died with him

The North Sea Empire was a personal union without unifying institutions; there was no common currency, no common court, no integrated administrative system, each realm retained its own laws and customs with only the king's person holding them together

Cnut's death in 1035 without a clear succession plan triggered competing claims from his sons Harold Harefoot and Harthacnut, whose short and mutually hostile reigns dissolved the empire before any institutional foundations could be laid.

sources.title: The New Cambridge Medieval History, Vol. V: c. 1198 – c. 1300

description: Germanic Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy (493–553) under Theodoric the Great, who attempted to preserve Roman administration under Germanic military rule; Theodoric's reign was the most successful example of barbarian-Roman synthesis, preserving Roman law, senatorial governance, and culture, before Justinian's reconquest extinguished this experiment in Romano-Germanic co-governance.

temporal.notes: Theodoric's kingdom; ended by Justinian's reconquest

lifecycle_phases.description: Theodoric the Great, king of the Ostrogoths, invades Italy at Byzantine Emperor Zeno's request to displace Odoacer (489–493). After a siege of Ravenna, Theodoric kills Odoacer personally at a banquet (493). He rules Italy as Zeno's viceroy in theory but as an independent king in practice. Rome's senatorial aristocracy, including Cassiodorus and Boethius, serve in his administration.

Theodoric's death (526) without a male heir triggers succession disputes; his daughter Amalasuntha is murdered (535), giving Byzantine Emperor Justinian a pretext for invasion. The Gothic Wars (535–554) are catastrophic: 20 years of fighting devastates Italy's economy and population. The final Ostrogothic king Teia is killed at the Battle of Mons Lactarius (554), ending the kingdom.

rise_factors.description: Theodoric's Roman-Gothic dual administration, Gothic warriors providing military security, Roman senators managing civil government, preserved Roman administrative infrastructure and made the Ostrogothic kingdom the most sophisticated Germanic successor state
Ostrogothic cavalry tactics trained in the Hunnic steppes were superior to the remnant military forces in Italy; Theodoric's decade on campaign before Italy had produced a disciplined, mobile army

Theodoric the Great deliberately preserved Roman civil administration, employing Roman senators like Cassiodorus and Boethius in key positions. This dual Gothic-Roman governance created a stable, prosperous state for three decades.

Control of Italy's most productive agricultural region, the Po Valley, gave the Ostrogothic kingdom a revenue base supporting both Gothic military elites and Roman urban populations, maintaining a prosperity exceptional for post-Roman Europe.

Theoderic the Great governed Italy by dividing military command between Goths and civil administration among Roman-educated senators, achieving a synthesis expressed in Cassiodorus's Variae that preserved Roman law and literacy under barbarian rule.

decline_factors.description: Theodoric's lack of a male heir created a succession crisis immediately after his death; his daughter Amalasuntha's regency was contested, and her murder (535) gave Justinian the pretext to invade

Justinian's reconquest campaign under Belisarius and Narses deployed the full military resources of the Eastern Empire; Gothic resistance was ultimately crushed by systematic attrition across 20 years

Justinian I's Gothic Wars (535–554) deployed professional Byzantine armies with Persian-trained generals (Belisarius, Narses). Despite Gothic resistance lasting 20 years, Byzantine resources ultimately overwhelmed an isolated kingdom.

After Theodoric's execution of Boethius and Symmachus (524), the Roman senatorial class shifted sympathy toward Byzantine reconquest. The executions destroyed the political compact between Gothic warriors and Roman administrators.

Justinian I's Gothic Wars (535–554) under Belisarius and Narses destroyed the Ostrogothic kingdom after 20 years of devastating warfare, depopulating Italy and leaving it more impoverished than any previous conquest had achieved.

sources.author: Amory, Patrick
sources.title: People and Identity in Ostrogothic Italy, 489–554

sources.author: Heather, Peter
sources.title: The Goths

description: Turkish frontier principality in Bithynia (c. 1299–1354) that seized Byzantine border territories as a gaza, holy war, state; Osman and Orhan's exploitation of Byzantine dynastic conflicts to cross into Europe (1354) transformed a minor Anatolian principality into the nucleus of an empire, demonstrating how internal Byzantine weakness enabled Ottoman expansion far faster than military strength alone could explain.

temporal.notes: Pre-imperial phase; transitions to empire with Constantinople conquest

lifecycle_phases.description: Osman I (1258–1326) leads a small Turkic beylik (principality) on the Byzantine frontier in northwestern Anatolia, near Bursa. The Ottomans attract ghazi warriors, fighters for Islam against the Christian Byzantine frontier, and rapidly expand at Byzantine expense. Orhan I (1326–1362) captures Bursa (1326), Nicaea (1331), and Nicomedia (1337), crossing into Europe at Gallipoli (1354) for the first time.

Murad I (1362–1389) conquers Thrace, defeats a Bulgarian-Serbian coalition at the Maritsa River (1371), and wins the pivotal Battle of Kosovo (1389), though he is assassinated during the battle. Bayezid I 'the Thunderbolt' (1389–1402) besieges Constantinople for seven years (1394–1402) and defeats a major crusade at Nicopolis (1396). His catastrophic defeat by Timur at Ankara (1402) reverses Ottoman gains temporarily.

The Ottoman interregnum (1402–1413) sees civil war among Bayezid's sons; Mehmed I (1413–1421) restores central authority. Murad II defeats another crusade at Varna (1444) and wins the second Battle of Kosovo (1448). His son Mehmed II 'the Conqueror' inherits a reconsolidated state ready to execute the long-planned conquest of Constantinople (1453).

rise_factors.description: The Ottoman ghazi ideology, holy war on behalf of Islam against infidels, attracted experienced warriors from across the Islamic world and gave Ottoman expansion a religious legitimacy that unified diverse Turkic groups; the sultans' role as defenders of Sunni Islam elevated them above other Anatolian beyliks

The Byzantine Empire was fatally weakened by the Fourth Crusade (1204) and subsequent Latin occupation; the restored empire (1261) could never fully recover its Anatolian heartland, and the competing Anatolian beyliks fragmented after the Mongol invasion, leaving the Ottomans as the dominant successor state

The devshirme system (Christian boys levied as soldiers) created the Janissary corps, professional infantry loyal only to the sultan, with no feudal ties, giving the Ottomans a uniquely reliable military force that could besiege cities and fight in all weather

The Ottoman beylik's location on the Byzantine frontier in northwestern Anatolia gave it first access to Byzantine Christian populations for ghazi (frontier warrior) raiding and conversion, attracting Muslim warriors seeking glory and plunder.

Osman I framed his campaigns as holy war (jihad) against Byzantium. This ghazi ideology attracted warrior volunteers from across Anatolia, giving the early Ottoman state a military manpower advantage over neighboring beyliks with purely dynastic armies.

Early Ottoman rulers accepted converted Christians into their administration and military as equals. This meritocratic system, unusual in contemporary polities, attracted talent and loyalty from populations who would have resisted pure foreign conquest.

Osman I's beylik attracted ghazi frontier warriors motivated by religious ideology as well as material gain, creating an army whose ideological commitment to expanding the House of Islam gave it cohesion and recruitment advantages over purely mercenary forces.

decline_factors.description: Timur's Mongol-Timurid army defeated and captured Bayezid I at Ankara (1402), dismembering the Ottoman state into competing successor beyliks; the interregnum (1402–1413) undid half a century of expansion

Timur's defeat of Sultan Bayezid I at Ankara (1402) temporarily dismembered the Ottoman state, releasing formerly absorbed beyliks and triggering an Ottoman civil war (1402–13). The beylik concept temporarily re-emerged before the Ottomans reunified.

The beylik's transformation into an empire under Murad I and Bayezid I required adopting Byzantine bureaucratic structures and a standing army (kapıkulu), ending the informal frontier-raiding culture that had originally defined the Ottoman enterprise.

sources.author: Reuter, Timothy (ed.)
sources.title: The New Cambridge Medieval History, Vol. III: c. 900 – c. 1024

description: Turkic Islamic empire (1299–1922) that dominated the Middle East, North Africa, southeastern Europe, and the Caucasus for six centuries; Mehmed II's conquest of Constantinople (1453) ended Byzantine continuity and positioned the Ottomans as the successor empire of Rome; their administrative devşirme system, legal innovations, and religious tolerance of dhimmi communities created the most durable Islamic imperial structure in history.

temporal.notes: Empire status from Constantinople conquest

lifecycle_phases.description: Mehmed II's conquest of Constantinople (1453) ends the Byzantine Empire and gives the Ottomans control of the Bosphorus. He reorganizes the empire on a systematic basis: the devshirme system provides Janissaries, the timar system organizes provincial cavalry, and the millet system governs non-Muslim communities. Selim I (1512–1520) defeats the Safavids at Chaldiran (1514) and conquers the Mamluk Sultanate (1517), making the Ottomans guardians of Mecca and Medina.

Suleiman I 'the Magnificent' represents the peak of Ottoman power. He captures Belgrade (1521), destroys the Kingdom of Hungary at Mohács (1526), and besieges Vienna (1529). The Ottoman navy under Barbarossa dominates the Mediterranean. Suleiman's legal codifications earn him the title 'Lawgiver' in the Islamic world. The empire stretches from Algeria to Mesopotamia, and Hungary to Yemen.

After Constantinople's fall, the empire systematically eliminates the remaining Christian states of the Balkans: Serbia (1459), the Byzantine successor states (Trebizond 1461), Bosnia (1463), and Wallachia becomes a vassal. Venice cedes Cyprus (1573 in later period). The empire reaches peak territorial expansion that defines the medieval-to-early modern transition.

rise_factors.description: Ottoman use of large-caliber siege artillery, including the massive bombards that breached Constantinople's walls in 1453, gave them decisive advantage over any fortification in Europe or the Near East; their combined-arms system (artillery, Janissaries, sipahi cavalry) was the most sophisticated in the world

The devshirme-timar-millet system created a uniquely efficient imperial administration: Christian slave-soldiers loyal only to the sultan, provincial cavalry paid in land grants rather than cash, and autonomous religious communities managing their own civil affairs, minimizing resistance while maximizing military output

Control of Constantinople gave the Ottomans command of the only sea passage between the Black Sea and Mediterranean; this chokepoint made the empire the mandatory intermediary for Black Sea trade and gave it leverage over Genoese and Venetian commercial networks

The janissary corps, slave soldiers recruited via the devshirme system from Christian populations, created a professional standing army loyal to the sultan rather than to competing Muslim noble families. This gave Ottoman sultans coercive capacity unavailable to rivals.

The millet system granted non-Muslim communities (Orthodox Christians, Jews, Armenians) legal autonomy over personal status law. This pragmatic tolerance enabled Ottoman rule over enormously diverse populations without the cost of forced conversion.

Mehmed II's capture of Constantinople (1453), using cannon to breach Theodosian walls that had held for 1,000 years, ended Byzantine civilization and gave the Ottomans the most psychologically significant capital in the medieval world.

Ottoman control of Anatolia's productive agricultural land, combined with the timar system that assigned land revenues to military service, created a sustainable fiscal-military system that Roman-Byzantine-style pay armies had never achieved.

decline_factors.description: Ottoman succession was decided by fratricide, the first act of a new sultan was typically to execute all male relatives; while brutal, this eliminated competitors, but the system created court factions around princes and harem politics that destabilized governance

By Suleiman's death (1566), the empire stretched across three continents; simultaneous military pressure from the Habsburgs in the west, the Safavids in the east, and the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean exceeded the administrative and logistical capacity of even the Ottoman system

Ottoman law effectively required new sultans to execute all brothers to prevent succession wars. While stabilizing individual successions, this practice repeatedly eliminated competent military and administrative talent, and created psychological pressure on the institution.
