sources.title: The Mongols

religion: Andean polytheism (staff-god lineage shared with Tiwanaku)

population_estimates.note: Wari resident-population estimate; total polity reach much larger.

description: Highland Andean state centred on the planned city of Wari in the Ayacucho basin, contemporary with Tiwanaku to the south and exercising influence across the central and northern Peruvian highlands and coast. Wari's hallmark provincial administrative centres at Pikillaqta, Viracochapampa, and elsewhere foreshadow the administrative infrastructure later developed by the Inca. Its collapse around 1100 fragmented Andean political space until the late Late-Intermediate Period emergence of Chimor and the contending Andean polities the Inca would absorb.

temporal.notes: Andean state centred on the highland city of Wari near modern Ayacucho; collapsed around 1100, broadly contemporary with the contraction of Tiwanaku to the south.

geographic.notes: Centroid set at the urban centre of Wari near Ayacucho.

lifecycle_phases.description: Wari city grows and projects administrative centres into central Peru.
Peak, provincial centres at Pikillaqta, Cerro Baúl, Viracochapampa active.
Administrative centres abandoned; Wari city declines.

rise_factors.description: Rectangular orthogonal administrative compounds at strategic provincial nodes prefigure Inca state design by five hundred years.
Upper Mantaro basin commanded routes between the Pacific coast and the Amazonian foothills.

decline_factors.description: Late-first-millennium drought (paleoclimate proxies) likely contributed to the abandonment of administrative centres.

sources.author: D'Altroy, Terence N.

description: Western Frankish kingdom (843–987) formed by the Treaty of Verdun under Charles the Bald; the continuous erosion of Carolingian royal authority through Viking raids, internal feudal fragmentation, and the emergence of powerful territorial princes reduced the monarchy to a shadow before Hugh Capet's accession founded the dynasty that would build the French state.

temporal.notes: Carolingian-era predecessor of the Capetian Kingdom of France

lifecycle_phases.description: Treaty of Verdun (843) creates West Francia as the western third of the divided Carolingian Empire, essentially modern France. Carolingian authority collapses under Viking raids; Charles the Fat cedes territory to the Vikings (Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, 911, creating Normandy). Hugh Capet's election (987) ends Carolingian rule and begins the Capetian dynasty.

Viking raids deepen the fragmentation of royal authority in West Francia; Charles the Bald's descendants prove incapable rulers, alternating with the more capable Carolingian kings of East Francia. The election of Hugh Capet in 987 ends the Carolingian dynasty in the west, establishing the Capetian line that rules France until 1792.

rise_factors.description: Carolingian sacred kingship and coronation by Reims archbishops gave West Frankish kings legitimacy; coronation unction with oil claimed to be from a divine dove made French kings uniquely sacred in the Latin world

The Seine, Loire, and Rhine valleys constituted the most productive agricultural land in western Europe; West Frankish kings could draw on this surplus to maintain the largest armies in Christendom and fund the monasteries and cathedrals that were medieval France's institutional backbone

Paris occupied a naturally defensible position on the Seine bend; it controlled river traffic, was easily supplied from the Île-de-France granaries, and was far enough from the frontier to be a secure administrative center, these geographic advantages made it the natural capital for whoever unified north France

The Capetians invested heavily in abbeys and cathedrals, Saint-Denis became the royal mausoleum, and in return the Church provided legitimacy, administrative capacity, and political support; the sacré of French kings at Reims connected them to Carolingian tradition

West Francia inherited the most sophisticated administrative infrastructure of the Carolingian Empire: Parisian ecclesiastical schools, the palace bureaucracy, and Carolingian chancellery traditions that survived the Viking crisis to become the basis of French royal governance.

The Seine and Loire basins, West Francia's core territories, were the most agriculturally productive regions in northern Europe. This agricultural wealth, combined with Paris's central position, gave West Francia recovery capacity after Viking devastation.

decline_factors.description: Viking raids devastated the Seine and Loire river valleys repeatedly from 840s; the inability of Carolingian kings to defend against raids transferred power to local counts who built castle networks; Normans established as permanent settlers in 911

Carolingian line weakened through premature deaths and minority reigns; Hugh Capet's election (987) as king despite the Carolingian claimant's survival shows how completely the dynasty had lost political authority

Viking raids along Seine, Loire, and Gironde rivers devastated monastic wealth, disrupted trade, and destroyed administrative networks; the inability of Carolingian kings to defend their subjects empowered local counts and bishops to take defensive initiatives that permanently shifted power from crown to locality

Repeated civil wars among Carolingian heirs (843 Verdun, 858 attempted deposition of Charles the Bald) diverted military resources from defense to fratricidal conflict; the nobility learned that backing rival claimants was more rewarding than loyalty, inaugurating the clientage politics that defined the Carolingian decline

The last Carolingian died (987), and Hugh Capet was elected king. This transition to the Capetian dynasty ended "West Francia" as a Carolingian concept, replacing it with "France", a new political identity centered on the île-de-France domain rather than imperial heritage.

description: Tangut state (1038–1227) founded by Li Yuanhao on the Silk Road crossing of the Hexi Corridor; the Western Xia developed their own Tangut script, administrative code, and Buddhist artistic tradition, and navigated between Song, Liao, and later Jin tributary pressures through skilful diplomacy until Genghis Khan's six campaigns destroyed it in 1227 and systematically exterminated its population.

lifecycle_phases.description: Li Yuanhao declares Western Xia state independent of Song and Liao; Tangut script created; Buddhist-influenced legal code issued
Western Xia controls Hexi Corridor, key Silk Road route between China and Central Asia; extracts tribute from both Song and Liao
Increased Song military pressure on southeastern frontier; internal succession conflicts; Jurchen Jin replaces Liao as northern neighbour
Six Mongol campaigns under Genghis Khan; Western Xia forced into submission (1209); final campaign ends with systematic destruction and population extermination

rise_factors.description: Western Xia's control of the Hexi Corridor allowed taxation of all Silk Road commerce between China and Central Asia
Western Xia military combined Chinese infantry tactics with Tibetan cavalry in a combined-arms force suited to the frontier terrain

decline_factors.description: Western Xia's geographic isolation made it impossible to find allies against Mongol encirclement; submission only delayed total destruction

description: Southern Arabian polities (various, medieval period) including the Ziyadi, Yufurid, Sulayhid, Hamdanid, Rasulid, and Tahirid dynasties controlling the incense trade routes and the Red Sea entrance; Yemen's mountain highland agriculture and monsoon-powered maritime commerce made it the wealthiest part of Arabia, with Aden serving as the key entrepôt for Indian Ocean trade while highland Zaydi Shia imamates maintained semi-independent governance against various lowland dynasties.

lifecycle_phases.description: Pre-Islamic Yemen was divided among Himyarite, Axumite, and Sasanian rulers before Islamic conquest.
Yemen became an early Muslim province; the region maintained its ancient trade identity alongside Islamic governance.
Series of local dynasties (Ziyadids, Yufrids, Najahids) governed Yemen semi-independently.
Rasulid dynasty created a prosperous, cultured sultanate; major patrons of Islamic architecture and agriculture.
Tahirid dynasty ruled until Ottoman conquest; Yemen remained a significant regional power through Red Sea trade.

rise_factors.description: Yemen's position at the mouth of the Red Sea made it indispensable for Indian Ocean to Mediterranean commerce.
Yemen's terraced highland agriculture (coffee, qat, wheat) produced surpluses that supported urban civilization.
Ancient South Arabian mercantile networks gave Yemeni merchants expertise and connections across the Indian Ocean.

decline_factors.description: Ottoman Empire conquered Yemen in 1517, ending indigenous dynastic rule.
Portuguese rounding of Africa disrupted the Red Sea spice trade that was Yemen's economic foundation.

description: The Mongol dynasty that ruled China from 1271 to 1368, founded by Kublai Khan after the conquest of the Southern Song. Capital at Khanbaliq (Beijing). Maintained Mongol administrative and military structures while adopting Chinese bureaucratic forms; oversaw renewed long-distance trade across Eurasia (Marco Polo era) and Mongol religious tolerance.

temporal.notes: Founded by Kublai Khan; ruled China after the conquest of Song; overthrown by the Ming dynasty in 1368.

population_estimates.note: Ethiopian highlands under Zagwe rule; medieval Ethiopian demography is poorly documented.

description: Christian Ethiopian dynasty (1137–1270) of Agaw origin that ruled the northern Ethiopian highlands in the interval between the long Aksumite decline and the Solomonic restoration; the Zagwe shifted the political centre south from Aksum to Roha (renamed Lalibela after their most famous king), and during the reign of King Lalibela (c. 1181–1221) commissioned the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela that survive as the dynasty's defining monument and as one of the masterpieces of medieval Christian architecture; the dynasty's claims to descent from Moses's grandson Akizana were always contested, and in 1270 a member of the Solomonic line, Yekuno Amlak, overthrew the last Zagwe king Yetbarak, founding the Solomonic dynasty that would rule Ethiopia until 1974.

temporal.notes: Christian Ethiopian dynasty between the Aksumite empire's collapse and the Solomonic Ethiopian restoration; centred on Lalibela in the highland north.

lifecycle_phases.description: Mara Takla Haymanot displaces the last Aksumite ruler; capital established at Roha in the central highlands; the dynasty consolidates control of the Christian north.
Reign of King Lalibela; commissioning of the rock-hewn monolithic churches at Roha (renamed Lalibela in his honour); contact with the Crusader states and Coptic Patriarchate of Alexandria.
Yekuno Amlak of the Solomonic line overthrows Yetbarak with the support of the monastic establishment; the Zagwe accept the new dynasty in exchange for retaining the Lasta region as a sub-kingdom.

description: Pre-Columbian Zapotec polity centred on the hilltop city of Monte Albán above the modern Mexican city of Oaxaca, with a continuous occupation from roughly 500 BCE through to the ninth century. At its Classic peak Monte Albán housed perhaps 25,000 residents and exercised regional dominance across the Oaxaca Valley through a network of fortified secondary centres. Its decline from around 700 onward preceded political fragmentation across the valley and the postclassic Mixtec ascendancy at Mitla and elsewhere.

temporal.notes: Classic Zapotec urban civilisation centred on Monte Albán above the Oaxaca Valley; political authority at the site contracted sharply by ~850, after which power dispersed to Mitla, Yagul, and smaller centres.

geographic.notes: Centroid set at Monte Albán.
